items.title: [RFC][KV Offload]: Align sliding-window restore coverage with MTP-retained history
items.body:
### Motivation

Native KV offload can report a sliding-window prefix hit and then try to load an older chunk that was never included in that hit. I reproduced both `Chunk ... not found in cache` and `Chunk ... is not ready for reading` through the real Python offload scheduler, CPU manager, and GPU block allocator classes, without concurrent eviction or any GPU kernel execution.

The trigger is `SlidingWindowSpec.extra_retained_tokens > 0`. `get_kv_cache_configs()` sets this to `num_speculative_tokens - 1` for multi-module MTP. That field extends the history retained by the block manager, but offload lookup and the producer's reachable-store mask still use the attention window without that extension.

This RFC asks whether the offload contract should cover the entire retained interval. My proposed first fix is to make lookup and store coverage match the existing allocation contract. The alternative—allocating only the attention-required interval on an external hit—needs a separate proof that later MTP replay and caching cannot read or publish the omitted history.

Source inspected and exercised: upstream main at [`fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/commit/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748).

### Reproduced failure

A small hybrid layout is sufficient:

- Full-attention group: 64 tokens per block.
- Sliding-window group: 16 tokens per block, attention window 32, extra retained history 3.
- One block per offload chunk, 16 tokens per hash, 65-token prompt, zero local cache hits.
- CPU cache contains the full-attention prefix and SWA chunks 2 and 3. SWA chunk 1 is independently missing, pending, or ready.

At the 64-token hit boundary, attention needs history starting at token `64 - 32 + 1 = 33`, within SWA chunk 2. The actual allocator retains history starting at `64 - 32 + 1 - 3 = 30`, within chunk 1.

| Extra history | Chunk 1 | Reported hit | Allocated SWA offsets | Load result |
|---|---|---:|---|---|
| 0 | missing / pending / ready | 64 | 2, 3 | succeeds |
| 3 | missing | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | `not found in cache` assertion |
| 3 | pending | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | `not ready for reading` assertion |
| 3 | ready | 64 | 1, 2, 3 | succeeds |

The missing chunk does not require an eviction race. For this hybrid layout, the real `_reachable_store_block_mask()` returns `[False, False, True, True]` at the 64-token boundary even with extra history enabled: the producer's filter itself omits chunk 1.

This is a bookkeeping reproduction, not a full model-serving reproduction. The prompt hashes and config objects are synthetic; `OffloadingConnectorScheduler`, `CPUOffloadingManager`, `BlockPool`, `FullAttentionManager`, and `SlidingWindowManager` are the actual implementations. No scheduler or allocator function is mocked. The target SWA descriptor is populated directly to isolate the retention contract; the probe does not instantiate an MTP drafter.

### Code path

1. [`get_kv_cache_configs()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/core/kv_cache_utils.py) tags sliding-window specs for multi-module MTP.
2. [`SlidingWindowManager.get_num_skipped_tokens()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py) subtracts `extra_retained_tokens`. Initial local-block adoption pads fewer null slots; external allocation therefore allocates the older retained block too.
3. [`get_sliding_window_size_in_chunks()` / `load_window_size_in_chunks()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/scheduler.py) omit that extension. Lookup reports 64 matched tokens without checking chunk 1.
4. `update_state_after_alloc()` starts from the first fresh non-null block, including chunk 1. [`CPUOffloadingManager.prepare_load()`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/fa1b3b1922ccb2d7a597925765c4bec7f358d748/vllm/v1/kv_offload/cpu/manager.py) then correctly rejects the unavailable chunk.
5. `SlidingWindowManager.reachable_block_mask()`, used by offload store filtering, also derives coverage from `sliding_window` alone.

### Proposed change

Keep the current allocator and MTP retention semantics. Make native offload coverage include every chunk that those semantics cause an external restore to read:

1. Derive offload lookup coverage from the retained interval, including partial-chunk alignment. Apply the same interval to the in-flight-load conflict check and relevant recency touches.
2. Extend the producer's offload store mask to supply that interval. Changing the lookup window alone would turn affected restores into misses because the producer can still omit the required chunk.
3. Keep the current outcomes: a missing required chunk shortens/rejects the hit; a pending required chunk defers lookup; a complete hit can be allocated and loaded. Preserve the existing `prepare_load` assertions.
4. Keep the actual model attention window, wire format, cache keys, and transfer ownership unchanged. No new user option is needed for an internal correctness contract.

The invariant is: **every chunk consumed by an admitted restore must be covered by the confirmed lookup, and every required chunk must be reachable through the corresponding producer store policy.**

A diagnostic baseline expands only the offload coverage descriptor from window 32 to 35 while preserving the real allocator's original `window=32, extra=3` spec. With this expansion, the mask becomes `[False, True, True, True]`; a missing chunk produces zero hits, a pending chunk defers, and a ready chunk restores 64 tokens successfully. All six `extra=0` controls are unchanged across the two modes. The script below checks all 12 combinations.

This descriptor substitution is an experiment, not the proposed production implementation. Production code should express offload coverage explicitly rather than changing a model's attention window. Wider coverage also has a cost: this example stores/loads three SWA chunks instead of two. It needs measurement, not an assumption that extra history is free.

### Validation before a PR

- Protect the confirmed missing/pending/ready behavior and zero-extra controls in the existing offload scheduler suite.
- Exercise a producer-to-consumer replay using actual store selection, CPU completion, lookup, and allocation; check that demanded keys were offered for storage.
- Cover chunk factors greater than one, unaligned hybrid hit boundaries, EAGLE tail handling, and in-flight loads with the same coverage invariant.
- Validate real multi-module MTP outputs and acceptance, plus cache bytes/hit rate and end-to-end latency on a prefix-reusing workload. These model/performance results have not been run and are not claimed here.

### Related work and duplicate check

Searched open PRs and issues for `extra_retained_tokens`, offload + retained history, multi-module + offload, and offload window/load coverage on 2026-09-13.

- #55818 addresses sliding-window allocation scaling and preserves extra retention; it does not align offload lookup/store coverage.
- #52287 addresses store windows moved by EAGLE's volatile-tail pop. This reproduction has no EAGLE pop.
- #56486 addresses a pending flag left behind by an invalid suffix. This reproduction has a complete reported hit and a later load failure.
- #54914 reports a similar load assertion under DSpark. I have not reproduced that deployment or established this mechanism as its cause; this RFC does not claim to resolve it.

### Feedback period

One week. The main decision is whether native offload should restore the entire retained interval, as proposed here, or whether initial external-hit allocation should distinguish retention-only history from the history required to resume. The latter must also preserve MTP replay and cache-publication correctness.

### Reproducer and environment

The 12-case diagnostic was executed with Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.11.0+cu130, the pinned Python source above, and existing precompiled extensions in WSL Ubuntu 24.04. No GPU kernels or model inference were executed. This is not validation on the repository's current PyTorch 2.13 dependency matrix.

Save the following as `retained_window_probe.py` in an installed checkout and run `.venv/bin/python retained_window_probe.py`. It writes a JSON result beside the script and checks the expected outcomes, including the two assertions in the unmodified path.

<details>
<summary>Executable 12-case diagnostic</summary>

```python
"""Exercise real offload lookup/allocation with MTP's retained SWA history."""

import json
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path
from types import SimpleNamespace
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

import torch

from vllm.distributed.kv_transfer.kv_connector.v1.offloading.scheduler import (
    OffloadingConnectorScheduler,
)
from vllm.v1.core.block_pool import BlockPool
from vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_manager import KVCacheBlocks
from vllm.v1.core.kv_cache_utils import BlockHash
from vllm.v1.core.single_type_kv_cache_manager import (
    FullAttentionManager,
    SlidingWindowManager,
)
from vllm.v1.kv_cache_interface import (
    FullAttentionSpec,
    KVCacheConfig,
    KVCacheGroupSpec,
    SlidingWindowSpec,
)
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.base import OffloadingKVEventsConfig
from vllm.v1.kv_offload.cpu.manager import CPUOffloadingManager


def probe(extra: int, older_state: str, expanded_coverage: bool = False):
    kv_spec = SlidingWindowSpec(
        block_size=16,
        num_kv_heads=1,
        head_size=1,
        dtype=torch.float32,
        sliding_window=32,
        extra_retained_tokens=extra,
    )
    full_spec = FullAttentionSpec(
        block_size=64,
        num_kv_heads=1,
        head_size=1,
        dtype=torch.float32,
    )
    groups = [KVCacheGroupSpec(["full"], full_spec), KVCacheGroupSpec(["swa"], kv_spec)]
    manager = CPUOffloadingManager(num_chunks=8)
    spec = SimpleNamespace(
        config=SimpleNamespace(
            groups=tuple(
                SimpleNamespace(group_id=i, tokens_per_block=g.kv_cache_spec.block_size)
                for i, g in enumerate(groups)
            )
        ),
        tokens_per_block=(64, 16),
        tokens_per_hash=16,
        blocks_per_chunk=1,
        offload_prompt_only=True,
        kv_events_config=OffloadingKVEventsConfig(
            enable_kv_cache_events=False, self_describing_kv_events=False
        ),
        get_manager=lambda: manager,
    )
    config = SimpleNamespace(
        speculative_config=None,
        cache_config=SimpleNamespace(
            enable_prefix_caching=True, prefix_cache_retention_interval=None
        ),
        parallel_config=SimpleNamespace(world_size=1, decode_context_parallel_size=1),
    )
    sched = OffloadingConnectorScheduler(
        spec,
        config,
        KVCacheConfig(num_blocks=32, kv_cache_tensors=[], kv_cache_groups=groups),
    )
    if expanded_coverage:
        # Diagnostic only: expand the offload coverage descriptor, preserving the
        # real GPU allocator's spec. This is not a production model patch.
        coverage_spec = replace(
            kv_spec, sliding_window=32 + extra, extra_retained_tokens=0
        )
        group = sched.config.kv_group_configs[1]._replace(
            sliding_window_size_in_chunks=(32 + extra + 15) // 16,
            kv_cache_spec=coverage_spec,
        )
        sched.config = sched.config._replace(
            kv_group_configs=(sched.config.kv_group_configs[0], group)
        )
    req = MagicMock()
    req.request_id = "replay"
    req.kv_transfer_params = None
    req.num_tokens = req.num_prompt_tokens = 65
    req.block_hashes = [BlockHash(f"block{i}".encode()) for i in range(4)]
    req.skip_reading_prefix_cache = False
    sched.on_new_request(req)
    state = sched._req_status[req.request_id]
    state.update_offload_keys()
    full_keys, keys = (g.offload_keys for g in state.group_states)
    ready = full_keys[:1] + keys[1 if older_state == "ready" else 2 :]
    store = manager.prepare_store(ready, state.req_context)
    assert store is not None
    manager.complete_store(store.keys_to_store, state.req_context)
    if older_state == "pending":
        assert manager.prepare_store([keys[1]], state.req_context) is not None
    external, async_load = sched.get_num_new_matched_tokens(req, 0)
    pool = BlockPool(32, enable_caching=True, hash_block_size=16)
    managers = [
        cls(
            kv_cache_spec=g.kv_cache_spec,
            block_pool=pool,
            enable_caching=True,
            kv_cache_group_id=i,
            scheduler_block_size=64,
        )
        for i, (cls, g) in enumerate(
            zip((FullAttentionManager, SlidingWindowManager), groups)
        )
    ]
    store_mask = sched._reachable_store_block_mask(
        sched.config.kv_group_configs[1], 0, 4, 4, ()
    )
    record = dict(
        extra_retained_tokens=extra,
        older_state=older_state,
        expanded_coverage=expanded_coverage,
        hit_tokens=external,
        async_load=async_load,
        swa_store_mask=store_mask,
    )
    if external:
        for m in managers:
            m.add_local_computed_blocks(req.request_id, [], 0, external)
        for m in managers:
            m.allocate_external_computed_blocks(req.request_id, 0, external)
        blocks = managers[1].req_to_blocks[req.request_id]
        record["allocated_offsets"] = [i for i, b in enumerate(blocks) if not b.is_null]
        try:
            sched.update_state_after_alloc(
                req,
                KVCacheBlocks(tuple(m.req_to_blocks[req.request_id] for m in managers)),
                external,
            )
        except AssertionError as exc:
            record["error"] = str(exc)
        else:
            record["load_jobs"] = len(sched._jobs)
            for job in sched._jobs.values():
                manager.complete_load(job.keys, state.req_context)
    return record


if __name__ == "__main__":
    records = [
        probe(extra, older, expand)
        for expand in (False, True)
        for extra in (0, 3)
        for older in ("missing", "pending", "ready")
    ]
    for r in records:
        if r["extra_retained_tokens"] == 0 or r["older_state"] == "ready":
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == 64 and r["load_jobs"] == 1, r
        elif r["expanded_coverage"]:
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == (0 if r["older_state"] == "missing" else None), r
            assert "error" not in r, r
        else:
            assert r["hit_tokens"] == 64 and "error" in r, r
    output = json.dumps(records, indent=2)
    Path(__file__).with_suffix(".json").write_text(output + "\n")
    print(output)
    print("All 12 diagnostic cases matched their expected outcomes.")
```

</details>

### AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with issue/PR searches, source inspection, the reproducer, execution, and this RFC. This is a design discussion with a verified bookkeeping failure, not a reviewed production patch or a claim of completed model validation.

items.title: [RFC]: Efficient Routed-Expert Replay with Prefix Omission and KV Cache Offloading
items.body:
### Motivation.

vLLM can return routed-expert IDs for replay and training. In multi-turn workloads, however, returning routes for the full prompt on every request repeatedly gathers, transfers, and concatenates historical data that the caller already owns.

Prefix caching avoids recomputing KV, but the routed-expert output path does not currently share the same ownership boundary. KV offloading makes this harder because a cached block may be restored to a different GPU block while the routed-expert table is indexed by GPU slots.

This RFC proposes prefix omission for routed-expert output and defines the compatibility contract for same-engine KV offloading, while preserving the existing behavior by default.

**Preliminary performance.** Step 3.5 FP8 on 8 × H200 (TP=8, PP=1), with async scheduling enabled and KV offloading disabled: 128 concurrent lanes × 100 turns, starting with 640 prompt tokens and adding 320 generated + 320 random tokens per turn, with a 1 s inter-turn pause. RPM includes these pauses; results are normalized to routed-expert return disabled. 

| Configuration | Mean latency (s) | RPM |
|-|-|-|
| Routed-expert return disabled | 5.695 (1.00×) | 1144.20 (1.00×) |
| Full routed-expert output | 6.642 (1.17×) | 999.29 (0.87×) |
| Prefix omission | 5.793 (1.02×) | 1127.64 (0.99×) |

### Proposed Change.

## Current behavior

Workers return routed-expert IDs with model output. `RoutedExpertsManager` stores them by full-attention GPU slot, gathers prompt routes with NumPy indexing, and appends decode routes to request state. The API returns the complete accumulated route sequence. Routed-expert return is currently rejected when KV transfer is enabled.

## Scope and non-goals

This RFC covers routed-expert prefix omission and compatibility with same-engine store/load KV offloading. Initial connector support targets SimpleCPUOffloadConnector, OffloadingConnector, and MooncakeStoreConnector. OffloadingConnector support is initially limited to the built-in CPUOffloadingSpec; TieringOffloadingSpec, secondary storage tiers, and custom offloading specs are out of scope. Prefill-decode disaggregation, `PP`/`DCP`/`PCP` greater than 1, more than two overlapping asynchronous scheduler batches, and the caller-side route storage implementation are out of scope for the initial implementation.

## Proposed API

Add `--enable-omit-prefix-routed-experts`. It is valid only with `--enable-return-routed-experts` and is disabled by default.

When prefix omission is enabled, vLLM omits routed experts for the cached prefix. The caller is responsible for receiving and retaining returned route chunks and correctly merging them with previously retained routes under the same session/cache identity. vLLM does not manage or verify this cross-request accumulation. 

The first completed GPU-plus-connector cache lookup sets `request.num_cached_tokens` as the immutable cached-prefix boundary. Scheduling, preemption, reset, and KV load may change computed or resident KV state, but must not change this boundary.

The returned range starts at:

```python
prompt_start = max(
    request.sampling_params.routed_experts_prompt_start or 0,
    request.num_cached_tokens,
)
```

## Internal design

**Prefix omission.** Slice the prompt slot mapping at `prompt_start` before the NumPy gather. This avoids materializing routed-expert data that will be discarded and leaves decode handling unchanged.

**Session isolation.** Use the existing request `cache_salt` mechanism to encode the stable session/cache identity in the first block hash, so shared prefixes, such as system prompts, are not reused across identities whose routed experts are owned separately. All three initial connector targets already preserve cache salt through their existing block-hash keys.

**Recovery after preemption.** The initial cache lookup remains unchanged and may combine GPU and connector hits. Once decode has started, routes for previously forwarded output tokens are retained in the frontend state of the same request, so recovery may use normal GPU and connector lookup. Before decode starts, recovery caps GPU prefix reuse at `request.num_cached_tokens` and bypasses external lookup. We will add a lightweight bypass hook to each of the three initial connector targets, preserving the initialization, state updates, and cleanup required for a zero-external-hit scheduling path without initiating a new external lookup or load plan.

**Offload safety (optional).** This proposal supports same-engine store/load offloading, not prefill-decode disaggregation. As an optional defense in depth, the scheduler may derive the routed-expert slots for the accepted external-token range from the allocated request block table. The scheduler invalidates these slots before the external KV load begins and reapplies invalidation after storing an older asynchronous output, without clearing slots for newly computed tokens outside that range. No routed-expert sidecar is transferred with KV.

## Alternatives considered

- **Always return the full route history.** This preserves current semantics but retains repeated collection and transfer overhead.
- **Transfer routed experts as a KV sidecar.** This restores historical routes with offloaded KV but substantially expands the connector protocol and data volume.

## Compatibility

- With prefix omission disabled, routed-expert output is unchanged.
- With routed-expert return enabled, KV offloading is supported only when prefix omission is enabled and the connector provides the external-lookup bypass capability. Both requirements are checked during server initialization; unsupported configurations are rejected, and every child of a composite connector must support the bypass capability.

## Risks

- **Cache identity consistency.** The three initial connector targets preserve the GPU cache identity, including `cache_salt`. This has not been established for other connectors; losing the salt during external key construction may allow cross-session hits and cause vLLM to omit routes the caller does not own. Requests without a stable session/cache identity are rejected rather than falling back to full routed-expert output.
- **Caller-side route reconstruction.** The caller must retain and correctly merge routes across requests sharing the same identity. Tokenization is not associative across independently rendered fragments, so route reconstruction must preserve alignment between expert positions and the corresponding tokens. vLLM does not verify the caller's retained routes or cross-request reconstruction.

### Feedback Period.

Two weeks.

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

Frontend concatenation of routed-expert chunks can block an API process when many requests finish together. Existing deployments can reduce this contention by increasing `--api-server-count`; this is operational guidance, not part of the proposed design.

A preliminary implementation is available in [this branch](https://github.com/cccyy123/vllm/tree/routed-expert-prefix-omit) for reference. Optional slot invalidation is not included.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC][Rust Frontend][gRPC] Split Control by caller and add --grpc-services
items.body:
## Purpose

The Rust frontend's `vllm.Control` service serves three different callers on one service name:

| Caller | RPCs |
| --- | --- |
| Router / gateway | `GetServerInfo`, `GetModelInfo`, `Abort`, `LoadLora`, `UnloadLora`, `ListLoras` |
| KV event consumers | `GetKvEventSources` |
| RL trainer / sidecar | `PauseGeneration`, `ResumeGeneration`, `IsPaused`, `Sleep`, `WakeUp`, `IsSleeping`, the five weight-update RPCs, `UpdateWeightVersion`, `GetWeightVersion` |

Functionally, clients that may call `GetServerInfo` can also pause, sleep, or load new weights in the engine. The gRPC port has no authentication ([security docs](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/usage/security.html#grpc-interface)), so in a typical enterprise deployment access is controlled by either strict network segmentation or a proxy or service mesh. Istio `AuthorizationPolicy` and Envoy RBAC match gRPC calls on `/package.Service/Method` ([Istio `Operation.paths`](https://istio.io/latest/docs/reference/config/security/authorization-policy/#Operation)). Maintenance of these policies is much simpler when matching on service prefix rather than raw verbs, and has the advantage of being forward compatible when new proto is changed/added.

The changes below would also enable selective configuration of mounted services, eg. not mounting paths that are unused, which is the most secure configuration possible.


This PR proposes:

1. **Three services in `control.proto`**: `Control` keeps discovery, `Abort` and LoRA. `KvTransfer` takes `GetKvEventSources`. `RlControl` takes the pause/sleep/weight-update RPCs. The messages are unchanged, and each service has its own impl over the shared `AppState`. The RL mutex is still a single instance.
2. **`--grpc-services`** chooses what is mounted on `--grpc-port`:
   - `all` (default): every service, same as today. RPCs for unconfigured features keep answering `FailedPrecondition`.
   - `configured`: `Inference` + `Control`, plus `KvTransfer` when ZMQ KV events are configured and `RlControl` when every engine has weight transfer or sleep mode.
   - an explicit list (`inference,control,kv-transfer,rl-control`): exactly that set. Startup fails if the list names a service the engines are not configured for.

   Unmounted services answer `Unimplemented`, and the health service only registers mounted ones.

   Mounting uses tonic's [`Router::add_optional_service`](https://docs.rs/tonic/0.14.6/tonic/transport/server/struct.Router.html#method.add_optional_service): each service is built only when its flag is in the resolved set. A `None` still claims the service name (tonic: "even when the argument given is `None` this will capture _all_ requests to this service name"), so calls to an unmounted service get `Unimplemented`, not a fallback route:

   ```rust
   let rl_control_service = services.contains(GrpcServices::RL_CONTROL).then(|| {
       grpc::RlControlGrpcService::from_arc(rl_control_impl)
           .max_decoding_message_size(DEFAULT_REQUEST_BODY_LIMIT_BYTES)
   });
   // ... likewise for control, kv_transfer and inference

   let svc = TonicServer::builder()
       .layer(middleware::request_runtime_layer(state.clone()))
       .add_service(health_service)
       .add_optional_service(control_service)
       .add_optional_service(kv_transfer_service)
       .add_optional_service(rl_control_service)
       .add_optional_service(inference_service);
   ```
3. **`ServerInfo.services`** (new `GrpcService` enum) reports the mounted set, so clients can check what is mounted instead of probing.
4. **Deprecated aliases**: every moved RPC stays declared on `Control` with `option deprecated = true` for at least one release and delegates to the new impl. It answers `Unimplemented` when its new service is not mounted.

With the default `all`, nothing changes for existing clients or deployments. `buf breaking` against `main` passes under `FILE` and `WIRE_JSON`.

### Other Motivating Factors

Draft PR #56337 (NIXL handshake over gRPC) stacks on this. It adds `GetKvTransferInfo` and `GetKvHandshakeMetadata` to `KvTransfer`. P/D peers need to call the handshake RPCs on each other's frontend, and they should not also be able to call `UpdateWeights` or other control surface methods.

llm-d and dynamo snapshot both have criu+cuda-checkpoint daemon implementations that need access to the sleep/wake RL lifecycle endpoints, it would be preferable to fence them off from other services. This enables a nice natural permission segmentation between the control surfaces needed by routers and serving orchestration tooling.

## Prior art

- etcd serves `KV`, `Watch`, `Lease`, `Cluster`, `Maintenance` and `Auth` as separate services on one port. Admin operations (defrag, snapshot, leader transfer) are in `Maintenance`, not `KV`. ([rpc.proto](https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/main/api/etcdserverpb/rpc.proto))
- Kubernetes CRI splits `RuntimeService` and `ImageService`. ([api.proto](https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/master/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto))

**Inference servers that keep one service (for contrast):**
- Triton's `GRPCInferenceService` puts inference, model repository load/unload, shared-memory registration and trace/log settings on one service, and gates them with flags such as `--model-control-mode`. ([grpc_service.proto](https://github.com/triton-inference-server/common/blob/main/protobuf/grpc_service.proto))
- SGLang's native gRPC server RFC puts generation, `PauseGeneration` and `UpdateWeightsFromDisk` on one service, and does not discuss access control. ([sgl-project/sglang#22558](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/22558))

**In vLLM:**
- #49491 renamed `vllm.Generate` (shipped in v0.22.0 through v0.26.x) to `vllm.Inference` in v0.27.0 without an alias. This PR keeps aliases for a release, which is the more conservative choice.
- `Control` grew by feature: discovery (#49491, v0.27.0), KV event sources (#50033, v0.27.0), RL lifecycle (#51316, v0.28.0), LoRA (#52840, v0.29.0). #51316 documented the RL RPCs as an administrative trust boundary on the unauthenticated port, and this PR gives that boundary its own service name.
- #49466 proposed an earlier Inference/Control split and was closed without discussion. Its changes landed through #49491.
- #51220 (RL endpoint parity for the Rust HTTP frontend) keeps the same RPCs behind `VLLM_SERVER_DEV_MODE`, which is the same idea: admin RPCs are not exposed by default.
- #42721 (API keys for the Python gRPC server) is about authentication and is complementary: per-service mounting limits what a caller can reach, while authentication decides who the caller is.

## Open questions

1. Should there be an `Events` service? 
    - `GetKvEventSources` goes in `KvTransfer` here because it is the only KV RPC today. Once #56337 adds the P/D handshake, `KvTransfer` would serve two different callers: routers and KV cache indexers read event sources, while peer engines call the handshake. Peers could then no longer be admitted with a single `/vllm.KvTransfer/*` rule, since that rule would also expose the event stream endpoints. A separate `Events` service for event-stream discovery (KV events now, possibly others later) would keep each service limited to one caller. Should that happen in this PR, or once there is a second event source?
1. When should aliases be removed? What is the right timeline for deprecation? One release (removed in the release after this lands), or tie removal to the gRPC API being declared stable?
1. What service mix is the right default if `--grpc-services` is unset, should we mount `all` or do auto `configuration`?
1. Should `KvTransfer` and `RlControl` move to their own `.proto` files, the way `inference.proto` is split out today?

## Test Plan

- `cargo nextest run -p vllm-server -p vllm-cmd`: service selection parsing and resolution, per-service mounting, `Unimplemented` for unmounted services, alias parity with the moved services, aliases following the mounted set, per-service health registration, and CLI/config snapshots
- `cargo clippy --all-targets -p vllm-server -p vllm-cmd -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `buf breaking` on `rust/proto` against `main`, with the `FILE` and `WIRE_JSON` rule sets
- `pytest -v tests/entrypoints/serve/grpc/test_grpc_services.py` (e2e, added to the Rust Frontend Serve/Admin job): starts `vllm-rs serve --grpc-port` with the default set, `inference,control`, `configured --enable-sleep-mode`, and an unconfigured `rl-control`, and checks the mounted set, `Unimplemented` on unmounted services and their `Control` aliases, per-service health, and the startup failure

## Test Result

- nextest: 478 tests run, 478 passed
- clippy: clean
- fmt: clean
- e2e: 4 passed in 125s on 1 GPU (Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B)
- `buf breaking`: passes under `FILE` and `WIRE_JSON`. Every RPC that exists on `main` is still declared on `Control`.

items.title: RFC: per-M, per-shape kernel dispatch for blockwise-FP8 linear layers (W8A16 at decode, FP8xFP8 at prefill)
items.body:
> **Scope caveat.** All measurements below come from a **single machine**: 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition (GB202, sm_120), PCIe peer-to-peer, **no NVLink**, driver 580.126.09, CUDA 13.0, vLLM `0.28.1rc1.dev500+g51da0ca66`, model Qwen3.6-27B-FP8 at TP=4. The *enablement* work is general; the *conclusions about where a change pays* are specific to a latency-bound interconnect and should be re-measured on NVLink before being trusted there. Numbers were produced by a harness that enforces CUDA-graph-captured timing, two working-set regimes (this GPU has 134 MB of L2), clearing both the vLLM and torch-inductor caches between A/B configs, node-level trace assertions for any wiring claim, and an output-equivalence gate.

**Status: draft, not filed.** Measured on 4× RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (GB202, sm120, PCIe).

## The claim

At decode batch sizes a blockwise-FP8 GEMM is **pure weight streaming**: it reads N×K weight
bytes regardless of how many tokens it serves, and the activation traffic (T×K) is two orders
of magnitude smaller. MMA throughput is therefore irrelevant there, so quantising activations
to FP8 buys nothing and costs a launch plus ~7× the numerical error. At prefill sizes the
tensor cores do bind and FP8×FP8 is the right kernel.

So the choice is a **regime** choice, and the regime boundary is per shape.

## Evidence

DRAM-resident (≥3× L2 rotating working set — the model's actual condition, since each weight
is touched once per step against ~6.75 GB/rank). Ratio is W8A16 ÷ (FP8×FP8 + activation quant):

| shape (per rank, TP=4) | T=1 | T=4 | T=32 | T=64 | T=128 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `in_proj_z` 1536×5120 | **1.21×** | **1.22×** | 1.05× | 0.73× | 1.21× |
| `in_proj_qkv` 2560×5120 | 1.12× | 1.13× | 1.01× | 0.78× | 1.07× |
| `linear_attn.out_proj` 5120×1536 | 1.08× | 1.09× | 1.00× | 0.83× | 0.66× |
| `gate_up` 8704×5120 | 1.04× | 1.05× | 1.02× | 0.94× | 0.67× |
| `down_proj` 5120×4352 | 1.04× | 1.04× | 0.98× | 0.85× | 0.74× |
| **T=256 / T=1024** (down_proj) | — | — | — | — | 0.58× / **0.54×** |

Accuracy is the unambiguous part: **2.3e-03…4.5e-03 vs 2.3e-02…3.4e-02** against an fp32
reference, ~7× better, because activations never leave bf16.

End-to-end, decode isolated, equivalence PASS at every point:

| batch | FP8×FP8 | W8A16 | delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 112.0 | **117.9** | **+5.3%** |
| 8 | 654.0 | **700.6** | **+7.1%** |
| 32 | 1983.5 | 2014.3 | +1.6% (noise) |
| 128 | 4144.3 | 3878.3 | **−6.4%** |

And W8A16 removes the activation-quant stage outright: **234 standalone quant kernel launches
per step → 0** (`per_token_group_quant_8bit` 127.4/step, `silu_and_mul_per_block_quant` 42.5,
three others), confirmed by node-level trace assertion.

## What this asks for

`linear_backend` is currently selected once, globally. The proposal is to let a layer hold both
prepared weights and pick per call by M, with the threshold **per shape** rather than one
global constant — `down_proj` turns over by T=32 while `in_proj_z` is still winning 1.05×
there.

The honest cost: no FP8-weight kernel in vLLM streams with bf16 activations from the CUTLASS
layout. Marlin needs `gptq_marlin_repack`; Machete needs `machete_prepack_B`; `torch._scaled_mm`
rejects bf16×fp8 outright. So per-M dispatch means **both formats resident**, and since the
Marlin repack is int32 and the same size as the fp8 original, that is **≈ +6.75 GB/rank** at
TP=4 for this model — real KV-cache budget. A kernel that streams FP8 weights against bf16
activations *without* a repack would remove that cost entirely and is the more valuable change.

## GB202 note

Two things specific to this part that are worth recording for anyone tuning sm120:

1. **The N tile is pinned by the quantisation block size.** CUTLASS asserts
   `Scale Granularity M must evenly divide the tile shape M`, and in the sm120 `swap_ab` decode
   path the tile's M dimension *is* the original N, with `ScaleGranularityM = 128` because the
   weight's block scales are 128 wide. So `ceil(N/128)` CTAs is implied by
   `weight_block_size=[128,128]`, not chosen — a 64-wide N tile will not compile. Adding CTAs
   via a stream-K/split-K scheduler instead measures **0.80–0.93×** the default scheduler at
   DRAM-resident working sets.

2. **Measurement traps that produce wrong tuning decisions on this SKU.** L2 is 134 MB, so a
   benchmark looping over one 22–45 MB weight is L2-fed and can read *above* the 1792 GB/s DRAM
   peak — that regime reports W8A16 at 1.81× where the DRAM-resident number is 1.04×. And
   per-call timing charges CPU dispatch to the kernel (23.94 µs vs 14.45 µs back-to-back for
   the same GEMM), which also makes two GEMMs on two streams look like they serialise when
   under CUDA graphs they overlap. Byte-weighted, these GEMMs run at 1000 GB/s in microbench
   and 1125 GB/s in-model — 56% and 63% of peak — so the remaining headroom is ~1.6×, not the
   2–3× the narrow shapes alone suggest.

---

### Corrections history

This work published several wrong numbers before the harness caught them. They are listed
because they change how the remaining numbers should be read, and because two of them are
traps specific to this GPU that anyone repeating the measurements will hit.

| claim | corrected to | cause |
|---|---|---|
| W8A16 is 1.81× at T=1 | **1.04–1.22×** DRAM-resident | 1.81× was L2-fed; this GPU has 134 MB of L2, so a loop over one 22–45 MB weight reads above the 1792 GB/s DRAM peak |
| GEMM launches serialise, so split-K is dead | GEMMs **overlap** under CUDA graphs | per-call timing charges CPU dispatch to the kernel (23.94 µs vs 14.45 back-to-back) |
| micro-batching costs +18–28 µs/GEMM | **+1.2–3.9 µs** | measured eager, and never measured the shared-weight L2 case that the second micro-batch actually sees |
| 381 standalone quant launches/step | **234** | trace window included prefill |
| GEMMs run at 27–48% of roofline | **56–63%** byte-weighted | the 27–48% shapes carry 18% of the bytes |
| the 256 KB two-shot threshold is too high | it is **2.5× too low** (crossover 640 KB) | fitted `comm(T) = F + B·T` rather than assumed |
| stream priority gives ~0 protection | **1.83×** with a real prefill background | the original probe used a wall-clock spin kernel, which measures queuing, not contention |

Two further results are negative and worth stating so others do not repeat them: collapsing the
second barrier of a two-shot into per-peer flag waits changes F by 0.7% (the cost is PCIe flag
propagation, not wait-for-slowest), and a grid-wide doorbell that cuts F by 30% in isolation
measures **−24.7% end-to-end**, because a grid-wide flag is a full grid barrier and waits for
the slowest-*scheduled* block once other work is resident.

items.title: [RFC]: P/D transfer contract across different parallel layouts with cp interleave size
items.body:
### Motivation.

The immediate motivation is P/D transfer involving DCP with token-level KV interleave (`cp_kv_cache_interleave_size=1`). A block-oriented transport can require whole-block interleave, while an attention backend may require or prefer a finer supported interleave. These are separate constraints: the connector should translate compatible layouts rather than force the attention layout to match its transfer unit.

#54803 gates the existing interleave adjustment on NIXL. #54734 explored connector capabilities for adjustment/validation. Neither defines a general direct-copy plan between different token/head/layer placements. This RFC asks for that design discussion, not another configuration-only fix.

The scope should be broader than one model or DCP pair:

| Producer → consumer | Placement problem |
| --- | --- |
| TP → DCP/I1 | Scatter the required tokens/heads into each consumer's local pages |
| DCP/I1 → TP | Gather distributed tokens into the consumer's required layout, including required replicas |
| DCP(D1, I1) → DCP(D2, I2) | Compose different token ownership and interleave mappings |
| PCP → DCP | Describe actual persistent KV ownership after prefill, then map it to decode ownership |
| PP → another PP/TP/DCP layout | Match layers independently of token/head ownership |
| DEP → DCP | Use the attention KV placement; expert parallelism is not itself a KV layout |

These are design targets, not claims that all combinations are currently supported. Only interleave values and cache formats supported by the endpoint backends are in scope.

### Proposed Change.

The proposed principle is:

> Backend/allocator adapters describe how local KV bytes map to parallelism-neutral logical coordinates. A shared planner composes those mappings. Connectors execute the resulting byte-copy plans.

The canonical representation is **virtual**: it identifies corresponding bytes, not an intermediate buffer that must be materialized.

#### 1. Reuse the existing mapping foundation, with a small shared contract

The offloading path already has `CopyRun` and `CanonicalPageMapping` from #48408 in [`vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/83fe99399ec0603b32393a14324b65c67ad04af2/vllm/v1/kv_offload/base.py#L465), with derivation in [`offloading/canonical_mapping.py`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/83fe99399ec0603b32393a14324b65c67ad04af2/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/offloading/canonical_mapping.py#L112). Can we share the byte-correspondence abstraction without making all connectors inherit offload storage policy?

An endpoint contract would distinguish:

- **Semantic format:** model/cache compatibility, layer and KV-component identity, KV dtype, quantization/scale encoding, and token/head geometry. Allocator group numbers and grouping remain endpoint-local.
- **Placement:** local tensor layout, token/head/layer ownership, replication, and local page geometry. DCP interleave belongs here. PCP adapters must describe stored KV ownership, not infer it solely from prefill compute partitioning.
- **Transport capabilities:** supported operations, registered memory, descriptor/submission limits, and completion semantics.

Topology-specific validation belongs in the vLLM adapter. The composition algorithm should consume validated ownership mappings rather than a growing matrix of TP/DCP/PCP/PP special cases. Source-replica selection should be a policy separate from byte identity.

#### 2. Compose mappings and bind explicit request coverage

Conceptually:

```text
source local bytes → logical layer/component/token/head coordinates
                                  ∩
destination local bytes → the same logical coordinates
                                  ↓
direct source/destination byte-copy runs
```

An affine run can describe source/destination offsets, fragment size/count, and strides. It must not assume the transport can submit an affine run as one native descriptor; the NIXL adapter may need to expand it into contiguous descriptors.

Request metadata should bind explicit logical token ranges to each endpoint's local page IDs, including prefix-cache hits, partial tails, and different page sizes. Alignment should not be inferred from block-list lengths alone. The abstraction should leave room for disjoint ranges and independently allocated stages rather than encoding a universal token-zero prefix assumption.

#### 3. Make segmented direct copy the default, including high fragmentation

The preferred path is direct transfer into the final destination KV pages. High fragment counts should result in bounded batches and pipelined submissions, **not automatically switch to GPU packing/unpacking or a local TP AllGather**. Avoiding extra GPU work competing with model forward is a primary motivation.

Optimizations to explore first:

- Compile/cache compatible layout-pair templates and validation results; bind addresses and clip ranges per request.
- Coalesce adjacent runs, generate descriptors efficiently, and reuse safe registration-dependent state.
- Bound queued descriptors and in-flight batches, with fairness across requests.
- Choose among equivalent source replicas using locality/load policy where useful.

Direct fanout may require sending the same semantic bytes to multiple consumers. This proposal does not claim to remove those bytes or that small transfers are free. We should measure CPU preparation, descriptor rate, IB throughput, and serving interference before deciding on additional execution strategies. An identical-layout contiguous fast path should remain available.

#### 4. Keep transfer lifetime separate from placement mathematics

We still need attempt identity, endpoint-generation checks, deduplicated completion, and a rule that a worker reports completion only after all its submitted fragments finish. Simplifying the interface must not weaken those guarantees.

However, byte mapping should not require the router to enumerate every destination process before prefill starts. Can existing connector handshakes and leases bind a producer transfer attempt to a destination session after the router selects decode, with membership cached once and compact per-request completions?

Lease expiry, aborts, retries, endpoint restarts, and outstanding remote reads need an explicit lifetime contract. A completion roster alone is not a proof that source pages cannot be reused while a remote read is outstanding. This is an open design question, not a proposal to replace the existing lease mechanism wholesale.

#### Scope and validation

Start with certified byte-compatible MLA/MHA layouts and NIXL, keeping the contract reusable by other connectors. Recurrent state, sliding/ring caches, incompatible quantization, and unknown layouts require explicit semantic adapters or rejection; they must not silently use attention-token mapping.

A staged implementation could separate shared mapping/composition, NIXL descriptor execution, and any necessary handshake/lifetime extensions into independently reviewable changes.

Validation should cover byte coverage and bounds, partial prefix/tail cases, interleave/page-size asymmetry, replicated destinations, PCP/PP ownership, and retry/abort/restart behavior. Hardware evaluation should measure cold versus warm planning, time to first submission, descriptor preparation, transfer latency/bytes, and model correctness plus P99 TPOT while transfers overlap decode. This RFC makes no hardware performance claim.

#### Open Questions

1. Is a connector-independent placement contract the right abstraction, and which parts of the offloading mapping should be reused?
2. Should semantic identity be per layer/component, independent of allocator grouping?
3. What is the minimal request-range and session contract that fits existing P/D routing and leases?
4. Which topology/layout pair should be the first end-to-end milestone, while keeping the broader use cases representable?
5. What performance gates should we use for highly fragmented direct transfers?


### Related Work

#33702 (NIXL roadmap), #54803 and #54734 (interleave adjustment/capabilities), #54496 (matching DCP layouts with PCP producers), #45340 (aligned PCP/DCP block accounting), #40674 (PP with NIXL), #48408 (canonical page mappings), and #38260 (multi-tier KV offloading). This RFC is about shared placement/composition and its execution contract, not replacing those efforts or claiming existing topology-specific work is unnecessary.

items.title: [DS-V4][SM80] portable Triton fallbacks so DeepSeek-V4 runs on Ampere/Ada
items.body:
## Goal

Let mainline DeepSeek-V4 **build and run on SM 8.x (A100 / A800)** without forking, by adding
portable Triton fallbacks for the parts that are SM90+/SM100-only today. Existing SM90 / SM100 /
SM110 paths are untouched — every change is capability-gated.

## Why this is needed

DeepSeek-V4 in mainline assumes SM90+: sparse MLA goes through FlashMLA/DeepGEMM, fp8 einsum
through DeepGEMM, MHC prenorm through tilelang/cutedsl, and several ops use the `float8e4nv`
Triton dtype. On SM 8.0 all of those are unavailable, so the model cannot even be constructed.
Ampere is still a very large installed base (A100/A800), so a portable fallback path is worth
having even at lower absolute performance.

## Design

Two layers, both selected at runtime by compute capability:

1. **Capability gates** (no behaviour change on SM90+):
   - `utils/import_utils.py`: `has_cutedsl()` returns False on SM8.x (cutedsl only emits SM90+ PTX).
   - `utils/deep_gemm.py`: `_use_sm12x_mqa_fallback()` extended to SM8.x; SM80 branches for
     `fp8_fp4_mqa_logits` / `paged` / `tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm`.
   - `compressor.py`, `sparse_mla.py`, `mhc/tilelang.py`, `flashinfer_sparse_mla_warmup.py`,
     `mla/{indexer,sparse_swa}.py`: skip cutedsl / DeepGEMM scheduler metadata / FlashInfer
     warmup where the arch cannot run them.
2. **Portable Triton implementations**:
   - `v1/attention/backends/mla/sparse_mla_env.py` (119 lines) + `sparse_mla_kernels.py`
     (3517 lines): the sparse-MLA decode/prefill kernels and the env switches
     (`VLLM_TRITON_MLA_SPARSE`, `..._TOPK_CHUNK_SIZE`, `..._QUERY_CHUNK_SIZE`,
     `..._HEAD_BLOCK_SIZE`, `..._MATMUL_DECODE`).
   - `models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/ops/sm12x_deep_gemm_fallbacks.py` (711) and `sm12x_mqa.py` (756):
     DeepGEMM / MQA fallbacks for SM8.x and SM12x.
   - `common/ops/*`: uint8-based fp8 conversion instead of `tl.float8e4nv`
     (`_f32_to_e4m3_uint8` / `_e4m3_uint8_to_f32`), plus the cache helpers the portable
     decode/prefill path needs (`dequantize_global_slots_k_cache`,
     `dequantize_combined_sparse_mla_decode_kv`, `sparse_prefill_combined_topk_size`).
   - `models/deepseek_v4/nvidia/flashmla.py`: SM8.x dispatch to the Triton path.

## Algorithm notes

- **Sparse MLA**: per query, gather the top-k selected KV slots (window + compressed + top-k
  indexer selection), then a flash-style online-softmax attention over those slots, with the
  head dim (512) split for the Triton tile. The portable kernels keep the same math as the
  SM90 FlashMLA path; they differ only in tiling and in decoding fp8/uint8 scales in software.
- **Indexer**: the scoring pass (`_indexed_d512_split_score/value`) is kept as-is; only the
  fp8 encode/decode changes to uint8 on Ampere.
- **fp8 einsum**: block-FP8 with 128×128 weight blocks and 128-wide activation blocks; scales are
  expanded to element-wise factors and folded into the fp32 accumulator (see #56119).

## Measured on A100 (SM 8.0), DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 2× A100-PCIE-40GB

The point of the PR is that the model runs at all; these are the numbers we measured once it did
(full report + raw data: <https://github.com/yeungtuzi/vllm-xtu-moe>).

**Prefill, single A100** (CPU experts vs layerwise GPU weight streaming):

| prompt tokens | CPU prefill | GPU prefill | speed-up |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 091 | 112.9 s | **5.6 s** | 20× |
| 4 137 | 439.4 s | **5.8 s** | 76× |
| 8 229 | – | **8.6 s** | – |
| 16 039 | – | **17.7 s** | – |

**Prefill, 2× A100 (TP=2 + expert parallel)**: 16 039 tokens in **13.96 s** (1 149 tok/s).

**Kernel-time breakdown of a 16 K prefill** (in-process torch profiler, per pass):
MoE kernels 31 %, elementwise kernels 29 %, H2D 19 %, dense GEMM 18 %,
**attention + indexer 2.9 %**.

**Numerics**: the portable kernels match a pure-torch reference to bf16 output precision
(RMS relative error 5.6e-3).

## Files taken from a fork

All new files and the adapted `flashmla.py` / `o_proj.py` come from the vLLM fork
[Lvllmds4-x](https://github.com/guqiong96/Lvllmds4-x) (Apache-2.0, author guqiong96). They are
byte-for-byte identical except for mainline API adaptations (e.g. `combine_topk_swa_indices` now
returns `(idx, lens)`). SPDX headers are retained. Debug instrumentation from our development
branch has been removed for this PR.

## Testing

- A100-PCIE-40GB (SM 8.0) + DeepSeek-V4-Flash: model builds, generates coherent text; the
  measurements above come from this configuration.
- SM90/SM100/SM110 paths unchanged (capability gates only).
- 21 files, +6 350/−119.

## Rebase note (2026-09-09)

Rebased onto `main@1454b71`. Upstream refactored three files we also touch
(`common/ops/{cache_utils,fused_indexer_q,fused_inv_rope_fp8_quant}.py` — new
`VllmTritonJitKernel`/`LaunchSpec` warmup structure), so our changes there were re-applied on top
of the new structure rather than merged verbatim: fp8 encode/decode via
`_f32_to_e4m3_uint8` / `_e4m3_uint8_to_f32`, `has_cutedsl()` gated with
`and not is_ampere_or_ada()`, and the ported SM80 kernels appended at the end of
`cache_utils.py`.

Verification so far: every touched file parses; the patch applies to `main@1454b71` with no
conflict markers. **A full A100 runtime validation against this exact rebased tree is still
pending** — I will report the result here before marking the PR ready for review.

## Related

- #56118 (CPU-offloaded experts), #56119 (o_proj fp8 correctness — required for correct output
  on SM8.x), and an RFC for layerwise GPU prefill of CPU-offloaded experts.

items.title: [MoE] add VLLM_EXPERTS_LOAD_DEVICE=cpu for GPU/CPU mixed expert placement
items.body:
## Goal

Make a MoE model whose **routed-expert weights do not fit in device memory** constructible and
servable in mainline vLLM, by keeping those weights on the host while everything else
(attention, router, shared experts, KV cache) stays on the GPU.

This is the enabling switch for a hybrid CPU/GPU MoE serving mode; it changes **no default
behaviour**.

## Problem

- DeepSeek-V4-Flash has 43 layers × 256 routed experts × **3.19 GiB** of raw MXFP4 weights per
  layer = **~137 GiB**. On a single 40 GB A100 the model OOMs *during construction*, before a
  single token is served.
- vLLM's existing offload machinery (`model_executor/offloader/prefetch.py`) moves weights that
  have already been constructed; it cannot prevent the construction-time allocation.
- Mainline has no way to say "build the routed-expert weights on the host". The MXFP4 oracle
  always prefers a GPU backend, which then fails with `b_q_weight is not on GPU` once the
  weights live on the host.
- ktransformers / lk_moe solve the same problem by keeping experts on the host and computing
  them on the CPU, which is what we do downstream — but they need a fork.

## Design

1. **`vllm/envs.py`** — new `VLLM_EXPERTS_LOAD_DEVICE` (`"gpu"` default, `"cpu"` opt-in).
   Orthogonal to `VLLM_TARGET_DEVICE`: the target device is still CUDA, only the routed-expert
   *parameters* live on the host.
2. **`routed_experts.py`** — when the switch is set, `create_weights()` runs inside
   `with torch.device("cpu")`. `create_weights()` allocates with no explicit device, so a scoped
   default device keeps the parameters on CPU from construction onward and the existing weight
   loaders copy into them in place. Everything else the layer owns (router tables, expert maps,
   shared experts) keeps its normal device.
3. **`fused_moe/oracle/mxfp4.py`** — with the switch set:
   - select the CPU backend unconditionally instead of preferring the GPU kernels, and
   - skip the AMX prepack, because the consumer is an out-of-tree CPU engine that reads the raw
     `[E, 2I, H//2]` / `[E, H, I//2]` uint8 weights and the raw e8m0 block scales directly.

   With `VLLM_EXPERTS_LOAD_DEVICE=gpu` (default) the oracle takes exactly the same path as before.

## Data layout the CPU backend consumes (context for reviewers)

| tensor | shape | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `w13_weight` | `[E, 2I, H//2]` u8 | MXFP4 e2m1 nibbles, gate rows `[0,I)` then up rows `[I,2I)` |
| `w13_weight_scale` | `[E, 2I, H//32]` u8 | e8m0 block scales (`2^(byte-127)`), groupK = 32 |
| `w2_weight` | `[E, H, I//2]` u8 | MXFP4 e2m1 nibbles |
| `w2_weight_scale` | `[E, H, I//32]` u8 | e8m0 block scales |

This is the checkpoint's on-disk layout, so no repack is needed on load — which is the point of
skipping the AMX prepack.

## Why this is useful (measured on our box)

2× A100-PCIE-40GB (SM80), AMD EPYC 9654, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, CPU experts + GPU attention:

| prompt tokens | CPU prefill (hybrid) | GPU prefill (layerwise weight streaming) |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2 091 | 112.9 s | **5.6 s** |
| 4 137 | 439.4 s | **5.8 s** |
| 16 039 | – | **17.7 s** |

The CPU path is what this PR enables; the GPU path (stream one layer's weights H2D, compute,
free) is a separate, out-of-tree mechanism. Full report, code and raw data:
<https://github.com/yeungtuzi/vllm-xtu-moe>.

## Testing

- 2× A100-PCIE-40GB + EPYC 9654, DeepSeek-V4-Flash + out-of-tree CPU MoE engine: the model
  constructs and serves where it previously OOM'd at construction.
- `VLLM_EXPERTS_LOAD_DEVICE=gpu` (default): unchanged behaviour, existing GPU backends unaffected.
- No kernel changes; the diff is three files, +59/−2.

## Related

- #56119 fixes DeepSeek-V4 `o_proj` on SM8.x (needed for correct output on A100).
- #56120 adds the portable SM80 Triton path so DeepSeek-V4 builds on Ampere at all.
- An RFC for a generic "layerwise GPU prefill for CPU-offloaded experts" hook will follow.

items.title: [Feature][Spec Decode] Add Uno shared-model drafting with a draft-only LoRA adapter
items.body:
## Purpose

Adds native Uno self-drafting through `speculative_config.method="uno"`. A single target model produces K draft candidates from one base-weight seed row and K−1 noise rows with the Uno adapter. The ordinary target verifier uses vLLM's existing rejection sampler and request-aware draft probabilities.

This implements the linear two-pass path discussed in [RFC #55267](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55267). The [contribution proposal](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/55267#issuecomment-5580777364) links the broader released integration. Before submission, the RFC and its comments were reread, and open-PR searches for the RFC number and Uno found no existing implementation PR addressing this scope.

The change includes:

- A dedicated proposer that shares the target model, attention layers and KV cache, with eager draft execution.
- Noise-only adapter routing and restoration of base-model mappings after drafting, including failure and startup-profiling paths.
- K lookahead KV slots, preserving correct ownership at full acceptance, block boundaries, preemption and prefix-cache reuse.
- Native dense draft-probability handoff through request reordering and trimming; the rejection sampler is unchanged.
- Startup and request validation, a Qwen3-8B serving recipe, CPU regression tests and end-to-end model tests.

Initial scope is a single NVIDIA GPU, synchronous Model Runner V1, text-only models with homogeneous full attention and the FlashAttention backend. The documented adapter is the original [Uno Qwen3-8B adapter](https://huggingface.co/s-sahoo/uno-qwen3-8B). Draft graphs, asynchronous execution, seed reuse, overlap and fused/tree drafting are separate follow-up changes.

Uno is introduced in [Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04010). The method and adapter are credited to its authors. This contribution develops the focused native integration from the public [Uno for vLLM v0.1.0 release](https://github.com/brntech/vllm-uno/releases/tag/v0.1.0); it does not inherit that release's full-stack performance measurements.

## Test Plan

Base: `5133e1d28594d5939552003f32b55a3fb18556a1`.
Contribution: `76f1eb3ebb4f5f6ed2ab206c31e16a5bdd2364d9`.
Tree: `5fd570e910e2bb8d8048361752230f2d817058f2`.

Tests were recorded at `efa9adc89a041427178e0d71715186edc5a25008`.
The submitted commits add DCO sign-off without changing any source tree.

Run from the source checkout using the uv-managed environment's Python. The recorded CPU environment used Python 3.12.3 and PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130 with no GPU visible.

Validation covers CPU configuration and lifecycle regressions, upstream lint and type checks, model parity and native rejection sampling on Ampere and Blackwell, and matched serving/model evaluations. Commands and the outcomes for each stage follow.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno.py \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno_config.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner.py \
  tests/v1/engine/test_preprocess_error_handling.py \
  -k 'uno or sample_passes_reordered_draft_probs_to_rejection_sampler or invalid_draft_suffixes_remain_rejected_in_metadata' -q

.venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/spec_decode/test_llm_base_proposer.py \
  tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py -q

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/worker/test_gpu_model_runner.py \
  -k 'sample_passes_reordered_draft_probs or dummy_sampler_run_warms_all_greedy_rejection_sampler or invalid_draft_suffixes_remain_rejected_in_metadata or is_uniform_decode' -q
```

## Test Result

Initial CPU results: **75 passed**, **106 passed**, and **4 passed**, respectively, on the original contribution tree. These suites overlap; the counts are not an aggregate of distinct tests. After GPU execution identified a startup-profiling cache-allocation issue, the focused Uno unit suite passes **26 tests** on the current tree. Its regression exercises native attention dispatch before and after cache allocation; both preallocation cases fail against the original implementation and pass with the fix. All applicable pre-commit checks pass, including mypy for Python 3.10 and the manual Python 3.12 hook.

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/spec_decode/test_uno.py -q

pre-commit run --files $(git diff --name-only 5133e1d28594d5939552003f32b55a3fb18556a1 HEAD)
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --hook-stage manual \
  --files $(git diff --name-only 5133e1d28594d5939552003f32b55a3fb18556a1 HEAD)
```

The GPU suite passes both cases on **RTX 3090 (Ampere, x86-64)** and **GB10 (Blackwell, ARM64)**, using the official CUDA 13.0 wheel for the exact upstream base:

```bash
VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 \
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/e2e/spec_decode/test_uno.py -v -s

.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/v1/sample/test_rejection_sampler.py -q
```

It compares matched LoRA-enabled base inference against Uno at K=1 and K=8, checks text and token IDs, exercises mixed-length chunked prefills, and repeats a reordered batch through warm prefix caches. Native metrics verify actual drafting, acceptance and cache engagement.

Each device passes all 12 exact output comparisons across the two cases. Both
also pass the 75 native rejection-sampler cases, including the target-distribution
test. The unchanged sampler was tested before the final startup correction;
model parity and serving checks used the corrected source. The RTX 3090 ran the
74 ordinary cases and the statistical case separately; GB10 ran all 75 together.

The separate RTX 3090 selectors were `-k 'not test_rejection_sampling_approximates_target_distribution'` and
`tests/v1/sample/test_rejection_sampler.py::test_rejection_sampling_approximates_target_distribution`.

The model is `Qwen/Qwen3-8B@b968826d9c46dd6066d109eabc6255188de91218`,
with `s-sahoo/uno-qwen3-8B@8819e09ac901e7290d8d89d62c98b9f756c602fe`.
Both serving arms use BF16, eager FA2, synchronous V1, batch invariance,
4,096 context, four sequences, a 256-token prefill budget, a 2 GiB KV cache,
prefix caching and LoRA infrastructure. Uno adds the original adapter and K=8;
the reference and target verifier retain base weights.

| Check | RTX 3090 | GB10 |
|---|---|---|
| GSM8K reference / Uno | 118/128 / 118/128 (92.1875% each) | 118/128 / 118/128 (92.1875% each) |
| Invalid answers / HTTP errors | 0 / 0 in both arms | 0 / 0 in both arms |
| Responses reaching the 256-token cap | 4 in each arm | 2 in each arm |
| Sampled comparison | 32 calibrated tests; minimum p=0.243969 | 36 calibrated tests; minimum p=0.114444 |
| Health, model listing, greedy/sampled chat, SSE | Passed | Passed |

GSM8K uses the first 128 questions, five-shot prompts, temperature zero, seed 42
and concurrency four. The public evaluator command, repeated for each server, is:

```bash
.venv/bin/python tests/evals/gsm8k/gsm8k_eval.py --port 8000 \
  --num-questions 128 --num-shots 5 --max-tokens 256 --temperature 0 \
  --seed 42 --max-concurrency 4 --save-results gsm8k-reference.json
```

GB10 calls the same upstream evaluator through a response-recording wrapper;
all 128 visible completion texts and predictions match. The RTX 3090 record
retains aggregate evaluator results. API output-token totals are retained
without normalization; this bounded validation introduces no throughput claim.

The sampled comparison uses 256 unseeded samples for each of three prefixes,
16 output tokens, temperature 1, top-p 0.95 and top-k 50. Both devices pass
their calibrated permutation comparisons at family-wise alpha 0.01 with
Bonferroni correction: no discrepancy detected at this sample size. The public
[sampling harness](https://github.com/brntech/vllm-uno/tree/b585483a8b6e79d22052389cf3c882afa90e0489/gates)
provides the client and comparator. The GB10 client also retains raw draft-counter
deltas, and supplies its saved Qwen3 prefix file as `--prefixes qwen3-prefixes.json`.
The RTX 3090 commands are:

```bash
python lossless_spec.py --url http://127.0.0.1:8000 --model Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
  --prefixes prefixes_spec.json --n 256 --chunk 4 --max-tokens 16 \
  --out sampled-reference.json
# Repeat for the Uno server, saving sampled-uno.json.
python lossless_spec_compare.py sampled-reference.json sampled-uno.json \
  --summary sampled-comparison.json
```

The GPU runtime uses PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130. Drivers are 580.65.06 (RTX 3090)
and 580.159.03 (GB10). Full tracked-source audits match the contribution tree;
all 17 x86-64 and 18 ARM64 compiled libraries match the official exact-base wheels.

## Contribution disclosure

AI assistance: OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude. The submitting contributor reviewed and approved this contribution. The tests and serving/model evaluations above were executed in AI-assisted development sessions; the recorded results identify their source, configuration and scope.

items.title: [Test] Conformance suite for cache_salt across OpenAI entrypoints
items.body:
## Purpose

Implements the entrypoint axis of #53194, the half left open when @oneKn8 took
the tier axis in #53769. Tests only; no production file is touched.

`cache_salt` partitions the prefix cache only if it survives the whole trip from
an HTTP request body down to the block hasher. `tests/v1/core/test_prefix_caching.py`
asserts that differing salts produce differing block hashes, but it builds
`Request` objects directly, so it begins after the plumbing that keeps
regressing.

Five cases over `/v1/completions`, `/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/embeddings`:

- same prompt under two different salts must not reuse blocks
- same prompt under the same salt must reuse them
- a request that omits `cache_salt` must not land in a salted namespace
- the pooling path, which rebuilds prompts before they reach the hasher
- the pooling path with chunked preprocessing enabled — a strict xfail, below

Assertions read `vllm:prefix_cache_hits` rather than
`usage.prompt_tokens_details`, which is only populated under
`--enable-prompt-tokens-details` and is hard-coded to zero on the pooling path.
Nothing inspects the extra-key tuple, so this is unaffected by #44706, #51899,
#52655 and #43789, each of which changes that encoding.

## What each cited bug gets

Being precise about this, since the motivation is broader than the coverage:

| Bug | Covered here |
|---|---|
| #47696 pooling drops the salt | yes — strict xfail, currently failing |
| #56199 empty salt shares the unsalted namespace | yes — strict xfail, found by @rishabhsinha17 reviewing this PR |
| #51818 Harmony tool turns | no — the Responses API is not exercised; its bug is a continuation, needing a multi-turn case |
| #51748 HF3FS external keys | no — connector tier. `HF3FSKVConnector` is a *declared* rederiver in #53769's exempt map with an evidence pointer, but nothing in-tree executes that path, since CI cannot import the hf3fs client |

The Responses, Anthropic `/v1/messages`, classification and scoring endpoints
also accept `cache_salt` and are not covered. Worth follow-up.

## #47696 reproduces on current main

`test_chunked_embeddings_isolate_on_salt` is `xfail(strict=True)`, so it flips
to a loud XPASS when #47696 lands. Controlled A/B, two identical pooling
servers differing only in `pooler_config.enable_chunked_processing`, two trials
each:

```
config                              diff-salt  same-salt   verdict
enable_chunked_processing: false            0        128   isolated
                                            0        128   isolated
enable_chunked_processing: TRUE           128        128   128 victim tokens served
                                          128        128   128 victim tokens served
```

One detail wider than #47696's description: the prompt is 256 tokens against a
1024 `max_model_len`, so it is never actually split. Enabling the flag is
sufficient — every pooling request takes the rebuild path and loses the salt
whether or not chunking occurs, rather than only long inputs being affected.

## Every negative arm is paired with a positive control

Load-bearing rather than stylistic, and I have the receipt. An earlier revision
of the third case asserted only the miss. Run against a server started with
`--no-enable-prefix-caching`, the other cases failed as intended and **that one
still passed** — it would have shipped asserting nothing. It now also asserts
that two unsalted requests share with each other, so the miss it reports is the
salt boundary holding rather than the unsalted path never caching.

## Verification

Run against real servers on CPU, at 13cf9e0:

```
4 passed, 1 xfailed in 57.10s
```

Mutation-tested by disabling prefix caching, where every non-xfail case fails.

Two details came out of running it rather than reading:

- The CPU backend reuses `--gpu-memory-utilization` to size its KV cache from
  host RAM and defaults to 0.92, so the fixtures pin it low to stay runnable on
  a developer machine.
- The block size is deliberately not pinned. Supported kernel block sizes differ
  per attention backend (`vllm/v1/worker/utils.py`), and a fixed `--block-size 16`
  passed on CPU while failing to start elsewhere. Nothing here needs to know it.

The pooling arms serve a causal model under `--runner pooling` with `LAST`
pooling, because prefix caching applies to pooling only for last-token or all
pooling with causal attention. A conventional bidirectional embedding model
would never engage the cache, and those arms would pass without testing
anything.

This file is standalone rather than importing `dimensions.py` from #53769, so
the two can merge in either order. Unifying them once both land would be an
improvement.

cc @oneKn8 @rishabhsinha17

items.title: [Feature]: Add RDMA-capable NIXL OBJ support for KV offload secondary tier
items.body:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

vLLM already supports an object-store secondary tier for KV offloading through the NIXL OBJ backend and OffloadingConnector (RFC for this: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38260). The existing JSON shape should remain the same: users configure an OBJ secondary tier with `type: "obj"` and provide object-store parameters through `store_config`.

I would like vLLM to extend this existing OBJ tier so it can use accelerated NIXL OBJ backends that support CPU DRAM registration and RDMA-capable object transfers.

Existing shape:

```json
{
  "type": "obj",
  "store_config": {
    "bucket": "kv-cache",
    "endpoint_override": "http://object-store.example:9000/",
    "scheme": "http"
  },
  "prefix": "",
  "io_threads": 4
}
```

Proposed extended shape:

```json
{
  "type": "obj",
  "store_config": {
    "bucket": "kv-cache",
    "endpoint_override": "http://object-store.example:9000/",
    "scheme": "http",
    "accelerated": true,
    "type": "<accelerated_backend_type>",
    "use_virtual_addressing": true,
    "req_checksum": "supported",
    "resp_checksum": "supported",
    "backend_params": {
      "custom_param": "custom_value"
    }
  },
  "prefix": "",
  "io_threads": 4,
  "max_dram_registration_bytes": 1073741824
}
```

Credentials and region should not be required in the JSON. They should be allowed to come from the AWS SDK default credential/config provider chain, including environment variables, AWS profiles, credential files, IAM roles, or workload identity.

Explicit access_key, secret_key, session_token, and region fields can remain supported for compatibility, but the expected production path should be environment/profile/workload-identity based configuration.

The vLLM-side changes should include:
  - Pass accelerated, accelerated backend type, checksum options, virtual addressing, and generic backend_params through to NIXL OBJ.
  - Preserve the existing OBJ tier behavior and object key layout.
  - Register the CPU primary-tier memory with NIXL for accelerated object transfers.
  - Support splitting CPU DRAM registration into multiple block-aligned descriptors using max_dram_registration_bytes, because accelerated NIXL OBJ backends may reject descriptors larger than CUOBJ_MAX_MEMORY_REG_SIZE.
  - Keep RDMA token handling, backend-specific memory registration, and object PUT/GET implementation inside NIXL.
  
This enables RDMA-capable object-store paths for KV chunks moving between vLLM's CPU primary tier and object-store secondary tier, without adding backend-specific transfer logic to vLLM.

### Alternatives

- Continue using the existing non-accelerated NIXL OBJ path. This keeps the current behavior but cannot use RDMA-capable object transfers.
- Add backend-specific RDMA/object-transfer logic directly in vLLM. This is less desirable because memory registration, RDMA token handling, and object transfer mechanics belong in NIXL.

### Additional context

This should be an extension of the existing OBJ secondary tier, not a new tier type.

The main implementation caveat is CPU DRAM registration size: vLLM currently has enough context to split the CPU primary-tier pool on KV block boundaries, while NIXL accelerated OBJ backends may enforce CUOBJ_MAX_MEMORY_REG_SIZE per registered descriptor.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: Application-Directed Prefix Checkpoints for Mamba / Hybrid Prefix Caching
items.body:
## Motivation.

> **TL;DR**: We propose an application-directed prefix checkpointing mechanism for hybrid SSM/Attention models (Qwen3.5, Nemotron-4, Jamba) in vLLM. By allowing applications to declare semantic prefix boundaries via an input-side control marker (`<|mamba_checkpoint|>`), vLLM coordinates Producer-Consumer prefill scheduling to eliminate redundant prefix computations across requests.
>
> **Key Production Results (Qwen3.5 35B on NVIDIA L40S)**:
> - 🚀 **+110.2% Throughput (2.1x Speedup)**: End-to-end serving QPS increased from **5.9 QPS to 12.4 QPS**.
> - 🎯 **Zero Accuracy Loss (100% Numerical Parity)**: Exact logit matching with eager baseline ($< 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ max diff in bfloat16).
> - ⚡ **48.6% TTFT Reduction**: Prefill latency dropped from 482 ms to 248 ms.
> - 📉 **53.4% GPU FLOPs Reduction**: Prefill computation cut from ~11,500 tokens/batch to ~5,358 tokens/batch.
> - 🏎️ **Up to 7.03x Kernel Speedup**: Batched phased GDN prefill kernel vs. legacy loop on L40S.
>
> **Evaluation Dataset & Workload Profile**:
> - **Structure**: 1-to-9 Multimodal Pairwise Matching benchmark (1 shared anchor item vs. 9 distinct candidate items, evaluated in 10-request groups).
> - **Prefix Anatomy**: Strictly identical shared prefix of $p \approx 624$ tokens post-expansion (structured text attributes + 1 high-resolution main image).
> - **Suffix Anatomy**: Diverging, variable-length suffixes ranging from 350 to 650 tokens (candidate text specifications + 1 candidate image). Total prompt lengths vary between 980 ~ 1,300 tokens.

#### Problem: The Memory & Boundary Dilemma in Recurrent Prefix Caching
Existing prefix caching in vLLM operates seamlessly for Transformer/Full-Attention layers where each token position independently retains a fine-grained $K/V$ vector. In recurrent models like Mamba/GDN, however, hidden states are sequential, stateful, and **substantially larger per checkpoint** (e.g., full $[H, D_k, D_v]$ state matrices per layer, ~512 KB per layer). Due to this memory footprint, recurrent architectures cannot afford dense token-wise caching and can realistically retain only **1 or 2 discrete state snapshots (checkpoints)** per sequence.

The core dilemma is that **from an engine-internal perspective, it is virtually impossible to heuristically predict where that single, high-value checkpoint boundary should be placed**. Geometry-based interval chopping frequently misses the actual shared premise or prematurely cuts across context. Conversely, **from the business application's perspective, this boundary is immediately obvious and trivial to locate** (e.g., precisely at the junction where a shared source item, document context, or system premise ends).

#### Real-World Workload: 1-to-$N$ Multimodal Item Matching
In high-throughput item matching pipelines (such as product deduplication and candidate item pair matching), a critical production task is **1-to-$N$ Candidate Item Matching**:
* **Input**: Given 1 anchor source item (`Item 1`), the system compares it against 9 candidate items (`Candidate 0` to `Candidate 8`), forming **10 item-pair inference requests** (1 Producer + 9 Consumers).
* **Multimodal Data**:
  - Each item contains rich textual metadata: item title, brand, manufacturer, and structured specifications.
  - Each item contains **1 high-resolution main product image** (`main image`).
  - Thus, every single request contains 2 images: `[Item 1 image, Candidate i image]`.
* **Output**: A sequence classification or scoring probability (logits) predicting whether `Item 1` and `Candidate i` represent the exact same physical product item.

#### The Variable-Suffix Geometry Problem
Each candidate item has distinct titles, varying attribute lengths, and different image aspect ratios/resolutions. Consequently, **the total prompt lengths across the 10 requests are inherently variable**:
```text
Request 0 (Producer): [Item 1 Text + Image 1] <marker> [Candidate 0 Text + Image 2_0] -> Total:  982 tokens (Suffix: 358 toks)
Request 1 (Consumer): [Item 1 Text + Image 1] <marker> [Candidate 1 Text + Image 2_1] -> Total: 1248 tokens (Suffix: 624 toks)
Request 2 (Consumer): [Item 1 Text + Image 1] <marker> [Candidate 2 Text + Image 2_2] -> Total: 1056 tokens (Suffix: 432 toks)
...
Request 9 (Consumer): [Item 1 Text + Image 1] <marker> [Candidate 9 Text + Image 2_9] -> Total: 1169 tokens (Suffix: 545 toks)
```

* **The Shared Invariant**: The prefix `[Item 1 Text + Image 1]` is **strictly identical** across all 10 requests (e.g., exactly $p = 624$ tokens post-multimodal expansion).
* **Full Attention Behavior**: vLLM's `BlockPool` easily aliases physical KV blocks for `Item 1` because token-wise attention vectors are independent of suffix length.
* **Mamba / GDN Dilemma**: Because Mamba recursively mutates its recurrent state in place, if all 10 requests are scheduled without explicit coordination:
  1. The engine cannot deduce where the common premise ends.
  2. Each request runs `Item 1` from scratch, wasting $9 \times 624 = 5,616$ redundant tokens per 10 requests.
  3. If requests attempt uncoordinated same-step execution, they either overwrite the shared live recurrent state (corrupting classification scores) or miss the cache entirely (`local_hit = 0`).

#### Why the Boundary MUST Be Declared by the Application Layer
