items.title: [RFC]: Optional native startup self-benchmarking for forward-pass performance characterization
items.body:
## Motivation.

Deployment planners, autoscalers, and inference optimizers need a small empirical performance model for the exact model, quantization, parallelism, CUDA Graph configuration, and GPU type being served. Static benchmark databases do not cover every combination, and external load generation cannot reliably construct exact internal scheduler coordinates such as:

- total uncached prefill tokens in one model execution;
- total KV tokens read by that prefill execution;
- decode batch size and aggregate decode KV depth;
- CUDA Graph capture boundaries and their eager fallbacks; and
- the largest points that fit the engine's actual model-length, scheduler, and KV cache capacity.

NVIDIA Dynamo currently solves this with a startup self-benchmark implemented in an out-of-tree vLLM scheduler subclass. The scheduler injects synthetic requests, builds a capacity-aware benchmark grid, runs the points before accepting traffic, and records one forward-pass metric (FPM) sample for each point. This implementation has proven useful, but keeping it out of tree has three costs:

1. It depends on private scheduler and KV-cache-manager details and must be updated for nearly every vLLM scheduler change.
2. It cannot be used by vLLM users that do not run Dynamo.
3. It duplicates lifecycle and timing integration that belongs next to the native engine implementation.

This RFC proposes moving the self-benchmark controller into vLLM. It builds on the native FPM proposal in [RFC #38760](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38760) and [PR #52061](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52061), so benchmark latencies use direct `execute_model` CUDA-event timing instead of a scheduler-side host-clock approximation.

The entire feature is optional and **off by default**. When no self-benchmark configuration is supplied:

- no benchmark grid is generated;
- no synthetic requests are created;
- no dataset is loaded or downloaded;
- no benchmark CUDA events, threads, GC policy, or result state are allocated; and
- the normal engine startup and serving paths are unchanged.

Self-benchmarking and external FPM publication are independent options. Enabling a self-benchmark temporarily enables the internal FPM collector and CUDA timer needed to measure benchmark points, but it does not require a ZMQ FPM port and does not publish synthetic benchmark samples to production FPM consumers. If external FPM publication is also disabled, the timer and benchmark-only state are released when the startup benchmark finishes.

## Proposed Change.

### 1. Activation and configuration

Add an optional `SelfBenchmarkConfig` to `VllmConfig`, exposed through a single structured CLI argument:

```bash
vllm serve MODEL \
  --self-benchmark-config '{"mode":"agg"}'
```

`self_benchmark_config=None` is the default and means disabled. A structured config is preferable to adding many unrelated top-level engine flags and leaves room for future benchmark policies without expanding the global CLI namespace.

An illustrative configuration is:

```python
@config
class SelfBenchmarkConfig:
    mode: Literal["prefill", "decode", "agg"] = "agg"
    output_path: str = "/tmp/vllm_self_benchmark.json"
    timeout_seconds: int = 900
    warmup_iterations: int = 5

    points_file: str | None = None
    prefill_max_new_token_samples: int = 64
    prefill_max_kv_read_token_samples: int = 16
    prefill_max_batch_size_samples: int = 3
    decode_max_kv_read_token_samples: int = 128
    decode_max_batch_size_samples: int = 128
    collect_imbalanced: bool = False

    kv_seed_mode: Literal["auto", "synthetic"] = "auto"
    prompt_content: Literal["random", "dataset_window", "dataset_chain"] = "random"
    kv_warmup_dataset: str | None = None
    kv_warmup_dataset_sha256: str | None = None
    kv_warmup_cache_dir: str | None = None
    giant_kv_threshold: int = 1_000_000
    giant_kv_repeats: int = 3

    gc_policy: Literal["default", "freeze"] = "default"
    gc_freeze_interval_seconds: float = 60.0
```

The names are proposed API, not a requirement to preserve Dynamo environment variable names. The values and behavior intentionally match the reference implementation where possible.

`mode="prefill"` runs only prefill points, `mode="decode"` runs only decode points, and `mode="agg"` runs prefill followed by decode. The name `agg` is retained for compatibility with existing Dynamo manifests; `all` would also be reasonable if maintainers prefer a clearer upstream name.

### 2. Startup lifecycle

The benchmark runs after model loading, KV-cache initialization, compilation, and CUDA Graph capture, but before the engine reports ready or accepts user requests. The proposed state machine is:

```text
DISABLED
   |
   | SelfBenchmarkConfig is present
   v
WARMUP -> PREFILL_SWEEP -> DECODE_SWEEP -> CLEANUP -> DONE
              \_____________________________/
                   selected by `mode`
```

The controller performs the following steps:

1. Read and validate the configuration or explicit point manifest.
2. Query scheduler/model/KV capacity and, under attention data parallelism, agree on a common capacity envelope across ranks.
3. Generate and validate the ordered point grid.
4. Run generic warmup and discarded eager-shape warmup points.
5. Run the selected measured prefill/decode phases.
6. Validate that the observed FPM shape matches the requested coordinate.
7. Atomically write a complete, partial, or failed result artifact.
8. Free all benchmark requests and KV, clear benchmark-created prefix-cache entries, restore GC policy, and release benchmark-only host state.
9. Enable normal serving and, if configured separately, production FPM emission.

The benchmark must not require a custom `scheduler_cls`. vLLM should expose a narrow internal scheduler adapter for capacity queries, synthetic request admission, decode steady-step construction, and cleanup. A custom scheduler that does not implement this interface should receive a clear startup configuration error only when self-benchmarking is enabled.

### 3. Benchmark coordinate model

The benchmark models the work performed by one model execution, rather than client concurrency or request arrival rate.

#### Prefill dimensions

| Dimension                | Meaning                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `total_prefill_tokens`   | Sum of uncached prompt tokens computed in the measured iteration.                                           |
| `total_kv_read_tokens`   | Sum of already-cached prompt/KV tokens read by the same requests. Zero represents a cache miss.             |
| `batch_size`             | Number of prefill requests in the measured iteration.                                                       |
| Per-request distribution | Equal split by default; an explicit manifest may request an imbalanced partition or exact per-request rows. |

For each request, `prompt_length = new_tokens + kv_read_tokens`. The generated grid splits both totals across the batch as evenly as integers allow. Nonzero KV reads are distributed in whole hash-block units so the cache lookup produces the exact requested coordinate.

#### Decode dimensions

| Dimension                        | Meaning                                                                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `total_kv_read_tokens`           | Sum of decode context lengths across all requests in the measured steady-state iteration. |
| `batch_size`                     | Number of decode requests, each scheduling one new token.                                 |
| Per-request context distribution | Equal split by default.                                                                   |

CUDA Graph mode, selected capture size, padding tokens, DP rank, and sample reason are recorded as metadata. They are derived from the coordinate and engine config; they are not independent Cartesian-product dimensions.

### 4. Generated-grid value selection

The default grid is deliberately structured rather than exhaustive. It preserves known performance discontinuities, spans the remaining range geometrically, and then applies configurable sample budgets.

#### 4.1 CUDA-Graph-aware axes

This rule is used for prefill `total_prefill_tokens` and decode `batch_size`.

Given configured capture sizes `C` and an engine-specific limit `L`, construct:

1. every legal capture size `C`;
2. every legal `C + 1`, because it is the first point that cannot use that exact graph and may select a larger graph or eager execution;
3. a geometric eager tail starting at twice the largest configured capture size; and
4. the exact engine limit `L`.

If CUDA Graphs are disabled, use powers of two up to `L` plus `L` itself. Duplicates are removed and the axis is sorted.

If the axis exceeds its sample budget, choose evenly spaced indices while retaining both endpoints. The implementation uses integer-rounded indices equivalent to:

```text
index(i) = round(i * (N - 1) / (K - 1)),  i = 0 .. K - 1
```

When values above the largest capture size are at most 20% of all candidates and fit within the budget, preserve the complete eager tail and spend the remaining budget uniformly on graph-covered values. This prevents a small but important eager region from being sampled away.

Default limits are 64 prefill-new-token samples and 128 decode-batch samples.

#### 4.2 Prefill batch sizes

For each prefill total-new-token value:

1. enumerate legal batch sizes from 1 through the minimum of the total tokens, `max_num_running_reqs`, and `max_num_scheduled_tokens`;
2. remove values that fail the full point-feasibility check;
3. keep power-of-two batch sizes and the exact legal maximum; and
4. take the first `prefill_max_batch_size_samples` sorted values.

The default limit is 3, normally selecting `[1, 2, 4]` when all are legal. This axis intentionally prioritizes small prefill batches instead of uniformly spanning to the maximum, matching the current Dynamo policy.

#### 4.3 Prefill KV-read values

For each `(total_prefill_tokens, batch_size)` pair:

1. If prefix caching is disabled, use only zero.
2. Binary-search the largest block-aligned aggregate KV read that fits model length, scheduler behavior, and live KV capacity.
3. Build a block-count ladder containing zero, one block per request, every power of two at or above the batch size, and the exact feasible maximum.
4. Convert block counts to tokens using the hash block size.
5. Uniformly limit the sorted ladder while retaining zero and the maximum.

The default limit is 16 KV-read samples per `(new tokens, batch size)` pair.

#### 4.4 Decode batch sizes and KV-read values

The maximum decode batch size is the minimum of:

- `max_num_running_reqs`;
- `max_num_scheduled_tokens`; and
- the number of minimum-size decode requests that fit in usable KV blocks.

The batch axis then follows the CUDA-Graph-aware rule in section 4.1.

For each batch size, binary-search the maximum feasible aggregate KV read. Build a candidate ladder from the batch-size minimum, powers of two, and the exact maximum. Each value is normalized to the coordinate the steady step actually measures, then deduplicated. Values below `2 * batch_size` collapse to the same effective coordinate because every request must be admitted with at least one computed token. The default limit is 128 KV-read samples per batch size, selected uniformly with both endpoints retained.

#### 4.5 Feasibility filtering

Generated points are admitted only when all relevant constraints hold:

- requested batch size and scheduled tokens fit scheduler limits;
- every request plus one output position fits `max_model_len`;
- chunked-prefill thresholds and hybrid block-alignment rules still schedule the exact requested number of new tokens;
- required KV blocks, lookahead slots, watermarks, sliding-window admission caps, hybrid groups, and recurrent-state reservations fit the live cache layout; and
- prefix-cache lookup behavior, including EAGLE/MTP cache-drop compensation where supported, produces the requested KV-read count.

Prefill points are generated in ascending-axis order and then executed from largest to smallest workload. Decode points remain ordered by batch and KV ladders unless real-KV warmup reorders them for chain reuse as described below.

### 5. Explicit point manifests and imbalanced batches

Users may provide an ordered JSON point manifest. An explicit manifest completely replaces generated sampling for the selected phases and is applied identically to all DP ranks.

To preserve existing Dynamo data and workflows, vLLM should accept the current versioned manifest semantics:

- schema v1: only aggregate totals; work is split evenly across requests;
- schema v2: a prefill `partition` may identify an axis (`new`, `kv`, or `both`), the number of high-work requests, and a fractional deviation; and
- schema v3: a prefill point may provide exact ordered `[new_tokens, kv_read_tokens]` rows for every request.

For example:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 3,
  "prefill": [
    {
      "batch_size": 1,
      "total_prefill_tokens": 1024,
      "total_kv_read_tokens": 0
    },
    {
      "batch_size": 4,
      "total_prefill_tokens": 1024,
      "total_kv_read_tokens": 4096,
      "rows": [[512, 1024], [256, 1024], [128, 1024], [128, 1024]]
    }
  ],
  "decode": [
    {"batch_size": 4, "total_kv_read_tokens": 8192}
  ]
}
```

Partitioned/row-based points conserve aggregate totals exactly. They isolate the incremental cost of within-batch imbalance without also changing total work. Exact rows are needed for calibration points whose per-request values must remain on one side of a kernel or launch boundary.

Imbalanced collection is itself optional and defaults off, even when such points exist in a manifest. With `collect_imbalanced=false`, uniform reference points are kept and imbalanced points are reported as intentionally omitted. This avoids paying for calibration-only forward passes in an ordinary sweep.

An infeasible user-specified point is a configuration error: the user requested that exact coordinate, so silently substituting another one would corrupt the artifact. Generated points may be filtered before execution because they are only the engine's proposed sampling plan.

### 6. Measurement semantics

#### Prefill

A prefill point is one measured model execution. Synthetic requests are created so the scheduler reports exactly the requested new-token and KV-read totals. The controller validates the observed FPM shape before saving the result.

#### Decode

A decode point uses two steps:

1. **Admission step, discarded:** admit each request at `max(1, context - 1)`. This includes new-request bookkeeping and is not representative of production steady-state decode.
2. **Steady step, measured:** schedule the same requests through the normal cached- request path, one token per request, at the requested aggregate context depth.

Only the second step is recorded. This produces a production-shaped `scheduled_cached_reqs` execution rather than measuring synthetic request admission.

The `wall_time` stored in the artifact is the native FPM `timing_scope="execute_model_cuda"` duration. Point construction, cache seeding, rank barriers, serialization, and cleanup are outside the timed interval.

There is an explicit drain cycle between coordinates so delayed timing samples from one point cannot be associated with the next one. Every saved sample is validated against benchmark ID, DP rank, request count, and token/KV totals.

### 7. Warmup policy

There are three distinct warmup mechanisms. The artifact should name them separately so users do not confuse model warmup with KV seeding.

#### 7.1 Generic model warmup

Before measured points, inject one request with a 256-token prompt and run one prefill plus `warmup_iterations` decode steps (default 5). These samples are discarded. This exercises the ordinary scheduler/model path after engine startup.

#### 7.2 Eager-shape warmup

CUDA Graph capture already executes captured shapes during startup, but eager-only shapes otherwise pay one-time kernel selection, first launch, and allocator growth inside their first measured sample.

For every distinct eager shape in the grid, prepend one discarded replica:

- key prefill warmup by total scheduled token count; and
- key decode warmup by batch size.

Keep these replicas adjacent to their phase and before the first real point of that shape. A failed warmup replica is logged and discarded; it must not turn an otherwise complete artifact into an invalid artifact. This behavior is already in Dynamo main through [PR #12176](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/12176).

#### 7.3 Real-KV warmup and seeding

[Dynamo PR #14029](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14029) addresses a larger fidelity gap for expert-parallel MoE models. Registering fake block tables does not execute the prefills that produced the KV, and all-zero or uniformly random tokens do not reproduce production expert routing. Deep-KV decode measurements can therefore differ materially from serving.

With `kv_seed_mode="auto"`, real-KV seeding is used when all of the following hold:

- the benchmark includes decode;
- the model is MoE;
- expert parallelism is enabled;
- prefix caching is enabled;
- no unsupported recurrent-state/Mamba KV groups are present; and
- the real-text dataset is locally available or can be fetched and verified.

Dense models and TP-only MoE models use the synthetic path because content does not create the same cross-rank expert-load sensitivity. Under attention DP, every rank reports eligibility and the group follows the least-capable rank so all ranks execute one identical plan. If auto mode is ineligible, collection falls back to synthetic KV and records the reason instead of silently mixing provenance.

##### Dataset and deterministic content

The reference implementation uses the ShareGPT V3 conversation dump with a pinned SHA-256. A user may instead provide a local file or an HTTP(S) URL. Remote custom datasets should require an expected SHA-256 and use an atomic, process-safe cache. Failure to fetch or verify the dataset makes `auto` mode ineligible; it must not hang startup indefinitely.

Conversation turns are concatenated into text. Entries shorter than 64 characters are discarded. A stable hash partitions conversations: the even half is used for collection and the odd half is reserved for held-out evaluation. The model's own tokenizer encodes text without adding special tokens.

Every synthetic benchmark request receives a unique `cache_salt`, so unrelated points cannot reuse or evict one another's logical prefixes by accident. For a prefill point with a requested KV read, only that point's seed request and measured request share a salt and a byte-identical token prefix. This makes the intended cache hit reproducible without allowing one measurement coordinate to poach another coordinate's cached blocks.

Each chain is deterministic. Its conversation order is shuffled from `(grid_digest, dp_rank, chain_index)`, and conversations are concatenated until the required depth is reached. Rebuilding a longer chain with the same identity yields the same prefix, allowing prefix-cache generational extension rather than recomputing the entire chain.

Measured prefill prompts remain salt-seeded random vocabulary tokens by default. Optional dataset modes select deterministic windows from a real-text token pool or reuse the same chain construction. In every mode, the selected token sequence is a function of the salt but not the requested length, so a shorter seed is a strict prefix of its longer measured request. Per-rank salt mixing prevents every DP rank from routing identical tokens to identical experts.

##### Chain planning and construction

Decode points are reordered by descending batch size and descending aggregate KV depth, while eager-warmup replicas remain pinned ahead of their corresponding real shape. For each batch-size rung, compute the deepest per-request context needed by its warmable points plus admission/steady-write headroom. Cap the target at model length and reduce it until `batch_size` chains fit in usable KV capacity.

For a rung of batch size `B`, launch `B` ordinary requests containing distinct real-text token chains. They run through normal chunked prefill. Stable cache salts and stable token prefixes allow later/deeper generations to hit cached blocks and compute only extensions. A chain is parked only after:

- `num_computed_tokens` reaches the full target prompt; and
- all asynchronous output placeholders/in-flight writes have drained.

Parking removes the chain from runnable scheduler state but keeps its request and real KV blocks resident. If any chain vanishes while a rung is being built, fail the whole rung, release surviving chains, and route all of its points to the synthetic fallback. A partial fleet must not be used.

##### Borrowed measurement shadows

For a warmed decode point, create one short-lived shadow request per chain:

- use the real chain's token prefix;
- share and reference-count complete prefix blocks read-only;
- allocate a private tail for the admission token and measured writes;
- use the manager's copy-on-write operation when available, otherwise zero-fill newly allocated private tail blocks; and
- register the shadow in every KV-cache manager so normal free/accounting paths remain valid.

The measured steady step performs no KV allocation. Cleanup uses the scheduler's fenced free path so a block is never returned while an in-flight GPU step may still write it. Parked chains and all benchmark-only tokenizer/text caches are released on success, timeout, or abort.

##### Repeated deep-KV measurements

PR #14029 proposes repeat protection for high-cost points because a single rare runtime pause can poison a row. The default threshold is 1,000,000 aggregate KV-read tokens and the default repeat count is 3. Run adjacent steady-state decode steps and store their median `wall_time`; record the actual `median_of` count in the artifact.

The current PR implementation also applies inexpensive repeat protection to all real-KV warmed points while limiting synthetic fallback repeats to points above the threshold. Whether upstream should retain that optimization or apply the threshold uniformly is an open question below.

Every result and skipped point records `kv_seed_regime`: `real_kv`, `fake_fallback`, `legacy` (warmup explicitly disabled), `skip:<reason>` (eligibility gate rejected the configuration), `unstamped` (the decode point never reached injection), or `not_applicable` (prefill). Run-level dataset and warmup-stage metadata are also recorded, so downstream consumers can reject mixed or low-fidelity regimes explicitly.

The evidence reported in #14029 comes from MiniMax-M2.7 on four B200 GPUs with TP4+EP. In that study, synthetic-KV points above one million aggregate KV-read tokens showed a median error as large as +160% in the static probe comparison, while real-KV-seeded collection reproduced previously validated serving-shaped coordinates to approximately 1%. A 147-coordinate repeated probe reported 0.54% anchor-reproduction MAPE. These results motivate the design but should be independently reproduced with native vLLM timing before changing defaults.

### 8. Optional benchmark-scoped GC policy

[Dynamo PR #12177](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/12177) addresses rare CPython generation-2 collection pauses during very large sweeps. In its reported 30k-point runs, full-heap walks grew from roughly 0.4 seconds to 9 seconds and a single worker pause stalled TP/DP lockstep, producing 3x-200x latency outliers.

This policy is a second-level opt-in and remains **off by default**, even when self-benchmarking is enabled:

```json
{"gc_policy":"freeze","gc_freeze_interval_seconds":60}
```

When enabled in EngineCore and every model worker:

1. save the existing generation-2 threshold;
2. set the generation-2 threshold to a practically unreachable value;
3. freeze the initialized heap;
4. periodically call only `gc.freeze()` from a daemon thread; and
5. leave reference counting and generation-0/1 collection active.

The periodic tick must not call `gc.collect()` or `gc.get_freeze_count()`: both walk large object sets and recreate the pauses the policy is intended to avoid. Cyclic garbage is intentionally deferred during the bounded benchmark window.

On every exit path, including abort:

1. stop and join the freeze thread;
2. restore the saved generation-2 threshold;
3. unfreeze and collect deferred cyclic garbage in an untimed window; and
4. freeze the surviving serving heap again, preserving vLLM's normal post-warmup GC baseline.

Worker restoration is part of the startup gate. A failure to restore one worker must fail startup rather than serve indefinitely with a benchmark-only GC policy. Because this code is native to vLLM, it should use direct worker lifecycle hooks or a bounded collective RPC; it does not need Dynamo's `worker_extension_cls` shim.

Native CUDA-event timing may reduce sensitivity to EngineCore-side GC compared with the current scheduler-host-clock implementation, but worker-side pauses can still leave the GPU idle between recorded events or stall distributed collectives. We should re-run the #12177 A/B experiment using native FPM timing before making any policy other than `default` the recommended setting.

In #12177's reported 30,480-sample A/B, the default GC behavior produced 25 outliers above 3x the coordinate median (0.082%) with a maximum pause of 8.9 seconds. The freeze policy produced 2 such outliers (0.007%) with a maximum of 1.131 seconds; those remaining samples were attributed to eager first-touch and are addressed separately by the eager-shape warmup. These numbers were collected with scheduler-side timing and therefore require the native-timing revalidation described above.

### 9. Data-parallel coordination

Each attention-DP rank first reports a capacity envelope containing:

- maximum model length;
- maximum scheduled tokens;
- maximum running requests;
- usable KV blocks with and without watermark reservation;
- a digest of grid-affecting scheduler/KV/CUDA-Graph invariants; and
- real-KV-warmup eligibility.

The common envelope takes the minimum numeric capacity across ranks and requires identical invariant digests. All ranks then build the same ordered grid and verify a common grid digest before execution.

Before a measured point, ranks use a bounded prepare/arm/go handshake. The barrier finishes before timing begins. The decode admission-to-steady transition does not add another barrier, matching production decode cadence; distributed collectives keep ranks aligned. Result collection verifies that every expected rank produced exactly one valid sample for the same benchmark ID. The group-level latency is the maximum rank `wall_time`, representing the critical path.

This coordination is only for coupled attention-DP/EP execution. Independent data- parallel engines may write independent rank artifacts without synchronizing their grids.

### 10. Timeouts and failure behavior

`timeout_seconds` is a soft startup budget, default 900 seconds. Once it expires:

- finish the currently measured iteration;
- stop only at a coordinated point/phase boundary;
- perform bounded cleanup;
- write a partial artifact; and
- continue startup if the partial artifact is internally consistent and usable.

A separate bounded cleanup grace prevents a failed rank or output write from hanging startup forever. Configuration errors, explicit-point infeasibility, cross-rank grid disagreement, incomplete rank results, failed cleanup, or failure to restore GC are fatal startup errors.

Generated-grid runtime failures may be recorded as skipped points, but the artifact must then be marked unusable unless the skip was an explicitly discarded warmup replica. The artifact must never present silently substituted coordinates as valid.

### 11. Result artifact

Write results atomically through `OUTPUT.tmp` followed by rename. For DP, write one rank artifact per EngineCore and optionally a merged artifact once all expected ranks are present.

The artifact should contain:

- schema version, artifact type, status (`complete`, `partial`, or `failed`), `valid`, and `usable`;
- run ID and ordered grid digest;
- start/end timestamps, elapsed startup time, and summed measured GPU time;
- complete configuration and negotiated capacity;
- CUDA Graph mode, capture sizes, expected capture size, and padding per point;
- expected/completed/skipped coverage and missing phases;
- measurement policy (`prefill=single_step`, `decode=steady_state_second_step`);
- generic, eager-shape, real-KV, prompt-content, and GC-policy provenance;
- one benchmark point plus its validated FPM sample per rank; and
- structured errors and skip reasons.

The existing Dynamo rank artifact uses schema version 2. Where practical, the native vLLM artifact should remain readable by existing Dynamo consumers; new map fields can be added compatibly. Any incompatible semantic change should use a new artifact version rather than changing existing fields in place.

### 12. Code organization

The implementation should keep benchmark-specific logic out of the normal scheduler and GPU hot paths:

```text
vllm/config/self_benchmark.py
    SelfBenchmarkConfig and explicit point-manifest schemas

vllm/v1/benchmarks/self_benchmark.py
    lifecycle controller, grid construction, validation, and artifact output

vllm/v1/benchmarks/self_benchmark_kv.py
    real-text dataset, chain planning/building, and shadow KV ownership

vllm/v1/benchmarks/self_benchmark_gc.py
    optional benchmark-scoped GC policy
```

EngineCore, Scheduler, and GPUWorker should contain only narrow optional hooks. The disabled branch should be a predictable `None` check and allocate no benchmark objects. FPM schemas/timing/publication remain owned by the existing native FPM module; self-benchmark code consumes that interface instead of duplicating it.

### 13. Initial support boundaries

The first implementation targets CUDA generative models. Based on current Dynamo behavior, the initial limitations are:

- no pooling/embedding models;
- no multimodal benchmark points;
- decode/aggregate mode does not initially support pipeline parallelism;
- decode/aggregate mode does not initially support speculative decoding, whose graph key also depends on decode query length; and
- real-KV shadow borrowing does not initially support recurrent-state/Mamba cache groups without private scratch-state support.

Unsupported combinations fail validation only when self-benchmarking is explicitly enabled. These limitations do not affect ordinary serving.

### 14. Implementation phases

1. **Native controller and parity:** generated/explicit grids, generic/eager warmup, prefill and two-step decode measurement, ADP coordination, cleanup, and artifact parity with Dynamo main.
2. **Real-content and real-KV fidelity:** incorporate #14029, including salted prompts, dataset provenance, chain seeding, shadow ownership, and repeat policy.
3. **Measurement hygiene:** incorporate #12177 as an optional, default-off GC policy after validating its effect with native CUDA-event timing.
4. **Dynamo migration:** switch Dynamo to the native vLLM config/result interface, retain only downstream result publication/consumption, and remove the custom scheduler implementation after parity validation.

Each phase should include byte/field parity tests against the Dynamo reference and GPU performance/fidelity tests covering sync/async scheduling, prefix caching, chunked prefill, CUDA Graph boundaries, TP, and attention DP/EP.

### 15. Alternatives considered

**Keep the implementation in Dynamo.** This avoids upstream surface area but leaves a large private-scheduler dependency and prevents non-Dynamo users from using it.

**Use an external load generator.** External traffic is useful for end-to-end serving benchmarks but cannot guarantee exact internal batch/KV coordinates or isolate admission from steady-state decode.

**Sweep every integer coordinate.** This is prohibitively slow and spends most measurements away from known graph/capacity boundaries. The proposed structured axes retain those boundaries and give explicit manifests to users who need exact points.

**Use only fake KV allocation.** It is fast, but #14029 shows that it can produce unrepresentative expert routing and deep-KV behavior on EP MoE deployments. It remains a labeled fallback.

**Always enable the GC policy.** This changes cyclic-garbage behavior and is not justified for ordinary serving or small sweeps. It remains a benchmark-scoped, explicit opt-in.

## Feedback Period.

Two weeks, or as maintainers prefer.

Specific feedback requested:

1. Should the upstream option be one structured `SelfBenchmarkConfig`, or should a minimal `--self-benchmark-mode` flag expose the common case?
2. Should `agg` be retained for manifest compatibility or renamed to `all`?
3. Should `kv_seed_mode="auto"` download a pinned default dataset after the user explicitly enables self-benchmarking, or require an explicit local dataset?
4. Should repeat protection apply to all real-KV points, as #14029 currently does, or only to points above `giant_kv_threshold`?
5. Should vLLM write only per-rank artifacts and let consumers merge them, or own the merged artifact for coupled attention-DP runs?
6. Does the optional GC policy still materially improve native CUDA-event samples, and which processes need it?

## CC List.

CC maintainers of the scheduler, EngineCore, KV cache manager, CUDA Graph, and FPM paths. Suggested names can be added after the initial design review.

## Any Other Things.

Reference implementation and related work:

- [Dynamo main self-benchmark configuration](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/backend_args.py#L318-L527)
- [Dynamo explicit point-manifest schema](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/benchmark_points.py#L13-L153)
- [Dynamo axis selection helpers](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L421-L516)
- [Dynamo generated prefill grid](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L2670-L3136)
- [Dynamo generated decode grid](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L3138-L3319)
- [Dynamo benchmark state machine and two-step decode](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L3794-L4133)
- [Dynamo artifact generation](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/eee249b2165b5508e1c65af0ace8d60162e7b61f/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L4149-L4453)
- [Dynamo PR #12176: eager-shape warmup](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/12176) (merged)
- [Dynamo PR #14029: real-text and real-KV collection fidelity](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/14029) (open at the time of this RFC)
- [PR #14029 real-KV warmup implementation](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/62c058a0aa86685180d543973e65b8490dd5f8d5/components/src/dynamo/vllm/instrumented_scheduler.py#L4134-L4874)
- [Dynamo PR #12177: benchmark-scoped GC policy](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/pull/12177) (open at the time of this RFC)
- [PR #12177 GC policy implementation](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/dynamo/blob/73bae73038310a1b970655159a0a3bfbfd27ec3a/components/src/dynamo/vllm/gc_policy.py#L1-L212)
- [vLLM FPM RFC #38760](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/38760)
- [vLLM native FPM PR #52061](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/52061)

This RFC intentionally proposes only native collection and artifact production. How Dynamo Planner or another consumer fits a latency model from the artifact is out of scope.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [ ] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the documentation page, which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [RFC]: fp8 KV cache gives little to no memory benefit on Mamba/GDN hybrid models
items.body:
**TL;DR**
- `--kv-cache-dtype fp8` roughly doubles KV cache capacity on attention-only models (measured 2.00x), but on Mamba/GDN + attention hybrids it gives 1.84x at 32k context and 1.00x (no gain) at short context.
- Root cause is the known hybrid page-pinning behavior (#37121, #40696): the Mamba state is not quantized by `--kv-cache-dtype` and all groups share one uniform page, so the bf16 Mamba page pins bytes-per-block and the fp8 attention page cannot shrink the pool.
- Fix is parity work: quantize the Mamba state too (SGLang already does this at int8) and/or decouple per-group page size (SGLang/TRT-LLM/llama.cpp already use separate pools). This RFC contributes the fp8-capacity characterization plus wiring a fix into vLLM.

### Motivation.

fp8 KV cache is advertised as a ~2x capacity/concurrency lever. On Mamba/attention hybrids (Falcon-H1, Qwen3-Next, Granite-4, Jamba, Nemotron-H) that lever is mostly or entirely dead, and there is no caveat in the docs. Numbers below are from vLLM's own `get_kv_cache_configs`/`get_kv_cache_capacity` (offline, no forward pass; `gpu_memory_utilization=0.85`, `max_model_len=32768`, default `block_size`, A10G). For Qwen2.5-3B and Falcon-H1 the offline bf16 result reproduces the live-served `GPU KV cache size` exactly, which validates the method; gpt-oss-20b is offline-computed and not anchored to a live run.

| model | bf16 KV tokens | fp8 KV tokens | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen2.5-3B (attention only, live-anchored) | 334,256 | 668,512 | **2.00x** |
| gpt-oss-20b (sliding-window + full, offline/unanchored) | 562,283 | 1,124,567 | **2.00x** |
| Falcon-H1-1.5B (Mamba + attention, live-anchored) | 603,229 | 1,111,381 | **1.84x** |

Falcon-H1 by context length: 512 tok 1.00x, 1024 tok 1.00x, 2048 tok 1.51x, 8192 tok 1.76x, 32768 tok 1.84x. Sliding window alone does not cause this (gpt-oss gets a clean 2.00x); the effect requires a non-attention group co-resident in the pool.

The mechanism is already filed. #37121 reports the ~7x KV memory over-estimation on hybrids: the attention block size is inflated up to the larger Mamba page, and the Mamba state is padded to match, so both grow to a common page. #40696 reports the prefix-caching consequence of the same block-size pinning. This RFC adds the fp8-capacity consequence and proposes the fix.

Why fp8 fails to help, concretely:
1. `get_mamba_state_dtype_from_config` returns bf16 regardless of `--kv-cache-dtype`, so the Mamba page is a fixed ~1.59 MB.
2. `get_uniform_page_size` asserts one page across all groups, and `_align_hybrid_block_size` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py`) enforces `attention_page >= mamba_page` by inflating the attention `block_size` (Falcon-H1: 1568 tokens at bf16, 3120 at fp8). The per-token attention page halves exactly under fp8 (1024 -> 512 B), so the block size roughly doubles (it lands one alignment step short of 2x), leaving the product pinned to the Mamba page.
3. Once pages are unified, `num_blocks` is effectively `available_memory // (uniform_page * num_groups)` (in code, `available_memory // bytes_per_block` where `bytes_per_block` is the max over groups of the summed page size). That uniform page is 1,605,632 B (bf16) vs 1,597,440 B (fp8) — essentially unchanged, so `num_blocks` moves only 405 -> 407. fp8's only gain comes from the larger block, dragged below 2x by the never-shrinking Mamba group and coarse block quantization (a short request fits in one attention block either way — the 1.00x rows).

### Proposed Change.

Two independent levers; either helps, together they recover the full 2x. Neither is novel — both exist in other engines — so the deliverable is the vLLM implementation plus the characterization above.

1. **Quantize the Mamba state alongside attention KV.** vLLM already exposes `--mamba-cache-dtype` / `--mamba-ssm-cache-dtype`, but the allowed values are only `auto/float32/float16/bfloat16` (no fp8 or int8), so today the state cannot be shrunk at all. This is the natural insertion point. SGLang ships state quantization at int8 (`--enable-int8-mamba-checkpoint`, `Int8CheckpointStore`, cited as ~2x prefix capacity), and Quamba2 (arXiv:2503.22879) quantizes the ssm_state at int8. Not yet done anywhere: fp8, and the conv_state (not just ssm_state). The recurrent path is the most quantization-sensitive component (Q-S5, arXiv:2406.09477), so this must ship with its own accuracy check (perplexity + one downstream task), not on an assumption of safety. Larger change: needs a quantized Mamba kernel path.

2. **Decouple per-group page size.** Relax the single-uniform-page invariant so an attention group keeps its smaller fp8 page instead of being inflated to the Mamba page; the pool tracks per-group bytes. This is what SGLang (separate `MambaPool`), TensorRT-LLM (separate cache managers), and llama.cpp (`llama_memory_hybrid`) already do via separate pools; academic cover in Jenga (SOSP 2025) and AVMP (preprint, arXiv:2605.22416). KV-cache-manager change only, no kernels.

Suggested phasing: (2) first as a self-contained KV-cache-manager PR that removes the pinning for the attention group (recovers most of the long-context gain, kernel-free). (1) as a follow-up that also shrinks the Mamba group, gated on the accuracy check. The characterization/probe can land as a test that asserts fp8 recovers ~2x on a small hybrid.

Out of scope: the sliding-window in-flight admission reserve (#54703, different mechanism) and block-pool logging (#54840).

### Feedback Period.

One week.

### CC List.

@heheda12345 @tdoublep

### Any Other Things.

Honest severity: the 1.00x rows are at short context, where KV is not the bottleneck, so the practical impact there is small. The impact that matters is long context, where fp8 under-delivers by ~8-16% on Mamba hybrids (1.84x vs 2.00x at 32k). Real and fixable, on a growing model class; not a crash or correctness bug.

Limitations of the measurement: one anchor hybrid (Falcon-H1) plus two attention-only controls. The mechanism is architecture-level (any non-quantized co-resident group pins the shared page), so it should generalize across Qwen3-Next/Granite-4/Jamba/Nemotron-H, but that is asserted, not yet measured per-model.

Reproduction (offline, no GPU forward pass, so it dodges any fp8 attention-kernel issues): build a `VllmConfig` via `EngineArgs.create_engine_config()`, construct per-layer `KVCacheSpec`s (Mamba shapes from `get_mamba_state_{shape,dtype}_from_config`), run `_align_hybrid_block_size` for the resolved backend, then call `get_kv_cache_configs` with a hypothetical `available_memory` and read `get_kv_cache_capacity`. bf16 reproduces live-served KV tokens exactly, which validates the fp8 numbers.

Not claimed as novel: the state-vs-KV asymmetry (Marconi, MLSys 2025), page decoupling (SGLang/TRT-LLM/llama.cpp, AVMP, Jenga), or int8 Mamba-state quantization (SGLang, Quamba2). The unpublished pieces are the fp8-capacity characterization on hybrids and, if pursued, fp8 + conv_state quantization with an accuracy frontier.

items.title: [Feature][Mamba] Support batch-invariant Mamba2 prefill and recovery
items.body:
## Summary

Support opt-in Mamba2 serving batch invariance, including preemption and recomputation, for a restricted Triton SSU configuration. Related tracker: #27433.

The original draft only fixed prompt factorization. As raised in [review](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54993#issuecomment-5529197609), that was insufficient: recomputing generated tokens through SSD does not reproduce their original SSU decode arithmetic. This revision preserves the original prompt/decode boundary and replays generated history through SSU.

## Implementation

- Execute original-prompt prefill as one model-configured scan chunk per physical SSD call, followed by the tail. For Granite's chunk size of 256, a 513-token prompt always uses `256 + 256 + 1`. This does not fix batch size or pad every request to 256 tokens.
- Retain original prompt lengths through both model runners. During recomputation, rebuild the prompt with the same SSD factorization and replay already-generated history using native multi-token SSU.
- Round the replayed SSM state to its cache dtype after each token, after computing that token's output, matching ordinary decode's state store/load behavior. Group mixed prompt/history rows without changing request or cache ordering.
- Keep ordinary decode on SSU; do not introduce a persistent partial-chunk replay buffer. Warm the added SSU launch variants through the existing Mamba warmup.
- Use the batch-invariant local mean reduction in TP gated RMSNorm. The previous eager local sum changed its floating-point reduction with row count for the tested TP configuration.
- Retain the one-attempt chunk-budget reservation after a chunk cannot fit. This can delay decode or leave budget unused; it is not a general fairness or latency guarantee.

All changes are gated by `VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=1` and actual Mamba2 cache groups where applicable. BI-off behavior remains unchanged. Mamba1 and GDN do not acquire support through this change.

## Supported scope and related work

This targets **the same request retaining its token IDs and logprob bits when batching or preemption changes, within the same execution configuration**. It does not establish general `prefill(prefix + token) == decode(token)`, RL training/inference alignment, equality between BI-on and BI-off, or equality across hardware, execution modes, or TP sizes.

Configuration checks reject non-Triton SSU, stochastic rounding, ReplaySSM, prefix caching, KV connectors, speculative decoding, and multimodal configurations. Token budgets and positive long-prefill thresholds must accommodate one scan chunk.

This continues the existing PR rather than duplicating #55627 / RFC #55524. Their exact-SSD-replay approach targets prefill/decode equivalence; this approach keeps ordinary SSU decode and reconstructs its history for serving recovery. The distinction was discussed [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/54993#issuecomment-5556260640). No comparative performance claim between the two implementations is made.

## Validation

Current head: `e82eebe4183b510c0dc260154a5bc4cc63f953ec`, rebased onto `c3ec0d29f54cdd450576d819b1e5229ce6ef080e`.

Environment: RTX 4090 (sm89), `ibm-granite/granite-4.0-h-350m`, bf16, PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130, Triton 3.7.1. The tested working-tree contents were matched to the committed files.

- **64 focused tests passed:** 55 single-GPU scheduler/cache/model-runner/recovery checks, 4 TP=2 recovery cases, and 5 gated RMSNorm tests.
- The real KV-pressure regression covers **TP=1/2 × eager/compiled × sync/async scheduling**. It exhausts a bounded KV pool without mocking allocation or invoking a reset API, asserts that a request with generated history was actually preempted, and compares token IDs plus fp32 logprob bits against standalone requests. Each case repeats the pressure workload twice and checks bounded completion.
- A separate regression forces repeated recovery and verifies that SSD prompt rows and SSU history rows coexist in a step.
- The focused TP norm negative control failed before the local-reduction fix and passes after it. The TP=2 eager real-pressure case likewise failed before that fix and passes after it.
- The SSU kernel suite previously passed **296 tests, with 18 skipped**, on `54e7409`; that SSU implementation is unchanged in the current head. One legacy-runner eager forced-recovery case also passed on that revision. The full eight-case pressure matrix above was run with the V2 runner, not both runners.
- Ruff lint/format checks and `git diff --check` passed.

<details>
<summary>Test commands</summary>

From the checkout, using the existing environment and locally cached model:

```bash
export PYTHONPATH=.
export VLLM_TEST_MODEL=/path/to/granite-4.0-h-350m
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/core/test_mamba_batch_invariant_chunk_split.py \
  tests/v1/attention/test_mamba_update_block_table.py \
  tests/v1/worker/test_mamba_hybrid_model_state.py \
  tests/v1/determinism/test_mamba2_preemption.py \
  -k "not tp2" -q
# 55 passed, 4 deselected

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/v1/determinism/test_mamba2_preemption.py -k tp2 -v
# 4 passed, 6 deselected

CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=2,3 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_mixer2.py -v
# 5 passed

# On 54e7409; SSU code unchanged in the current head:
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 .venv/bin/python -m pytest \
  tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_ssm.py -q
# 296 passed, 18 skipped

.venv/bin/python -m ruff check \
  tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_mixer2.py \
  tests/v1/determinism/test_mamba2_preemption.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/mamba_mixer2.py
.venv/bin/python -m ruff format --check \
  tests/kernels/mamba/test_mamba_mixer2.py \
  tests/v1/determinism/test_mamba2_preemption.py \
  vllm/model_executor/layers/mamba/mamba_mixer2.py
git diff --check
```

</details>

These are model-level serving determinism checks, not a full upstream CI result or a task-accuracy benchmark. Broader model/architecture coverage, including larger or pure-Mamba2 models and Hopper/Blackwell serving, remains unverified.

## Performance and exact-replay trade-off

I also ran a direct same-base comparison with the core exact-SSD-replay implementation from #55627. Commit `7986c8c` from that PR cherry-picked cleanly onto `c3ec0d2`, which is also the base of this PR; this PR was tested at `e82eebe`. The exact-replay focused kernel, metadata, and configuration tests passed **36/36** after the port.

The benchmark used one RTX 4090, Granite-4.0-H-350M bf16, TP=1, compiled mode, async scheduling, prefix caching off, 32 maximum sequences, and a 1024-token scheduler budget. Each table entry is the mean of two independent engine lifetimes. Within each workload the run order was BI-off / this PR / exact replay / exact replay / this PR / BI-off.

| Input / output tokens | Requests | BI off | This PR | Exact SSD replay | This PR throughput vs exact replay |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2048 / 64 | 128 | 8.141 s (15.72 req/s) | 8.917 s (14.35 req/s) | 14.661 s (8.73 req/s) | 1.64x |
| 128 / 256 | 64 | 1.620 s (39.51 req/s) | 3.442 s (18.60 req/s) | 14.003 s (4.57 req/s) | 4.07x |

Relative to BI off, this PR increased whole-batch elapsed time by 9.5% in the long-prefill workload and 112.5% in the decode-heavy workload. Exact replay increased it by 80.1% and 764.4%, respectively. These figures include the cost of the complete BI path, including the batch-invariant linear implementation; they do not isolate scheduler overhead.

With the same `gpu_memory_utilization=0.25` and 2304-token maximum model length, the startup cache planner reported:

| Variant | Attention page size | Planned cache capacity | Reported maximum concurrency at 2304 tokens |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BI off | 400 tokens | 575,291 tokens | 249.69x |
| This PR | 400 tokens | 582,380 tokens | 252.77x |
| Exact SSD replay | 1712 tokens | 197,376 tokens | 85.67x |

The small BI-off versus this-PR capacity difference is profiling variance; both retain the existing two-tensor Mamba state layout. Exact replay adds an fp32 boundary state and four partial-chunk buffers, enlarging the unified cache page for this model. These are planner-reported capacities, not direct peak-memory measurements.

The two approaches deliberately provide different contracts:

- **This PR is serving-oriented.** Original prompt tokens retain a fixed physical SSD factorization, ordinary decode remains on SSU, and generated history is replayed through rounded SSU only during recovery. This reduces steady-state decode and cache costs and has been tested with TP=2. The trade-off is stronger scheduler coupling: fixed prompt chunks and the one-attempt reservation can delay decode or leave token budget unused. It preserves a request across supported batching and recovery changes, but does not claim general prefill/decode equivalence.
- **#55627 provides the stronger path-equivalence contract.** Replaying from a canonical SSD chunk boundary permits arbitrary scheduler split points and makes prefill, chunked prefill, and decode agree. That is useful when a generated sequence must be reproduced through prefill, including training/inference or RL logprob alignment. The current implementation pays for partial-chunk SSD replay on every decode step, stores the additional replay state, runs Mamba2 outside full CUDA graphs, and currently rejects TP/PP greater than one.

The measurements therefore do not establish a universal winner: exact replay offers a stronger semantic guarantee, while this PR evaluates the lower-cost contract needed for online serving determinism.

<details>
<summary>Benchmark command</summary>

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 \
VLLM_BATCH_INVARIANT=<0-or-1> \
VLLM_USE_FLASHINFER_SAMPLER=0 \
VLLM_ENABLE_V1_MULTIPROCESSING=0 OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 \
.venv/bin/python -m vllm.entrypoints.cli.main bench throughput \
  --model /path/to/granite-4.0-h-350m --dtype bfloat16 \
  --dataset-name random --random-input-len <2048-or-128> \
  --random-output-len <64-or-256> --random-range-ratio 0 \
  --num-prompts <128-or-64> --num-warmups <32-or-16> \
  --max-model-len <2304-or-512> --max-num-seqs 32 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 1024 --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --no-enable-prefix-caching --async-scheduling \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.25 --disable-detokenize --seed 42 \
  --output-json /path/to/result.json
```

</details>

These are small, offline whole-batch measurements on one model/GPU, not production TTFT/ITL/P99, a model-quality evaluation, or a universal BI overhead estimate. They do not compare the approaches on Hopper/Blackwell or larger and pure-Mamba2 models.

## AI assistance

OpenAI Codex assisted with investigation, implementation, test execution, and preparation of this description.

items.title: [Test][RL] Add sleep/wake E2E suite with MRV1/MRV2 runner matrix
items.body:
## Purpose

Add end-to-end guard tests for the vLLM sleep-mode lifecycle (`POST /sleep`, `POST /wake_up`, `GET /is_sleeping`), rebuilt on top of the (now closed) #45586 draft — its pause/resume portion already landed via #52144; this PR revives the sleep/wake portion.

- 27 single-dimension tests, each running on **both MRV1 and MRV2** (54 collected instances) via an explicit `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` parametrized fixture — both values are set explicitly because recent vLLM defaults to MRV2, so an unset variable would silently run both rounds on MRV2
- three fixture tiers (class-scoped shared / function-scoped isolated / seeded) keep exactly one server alive at any moment: 32 starts serve 54 instances
- mechanism-layer thresholds centralized in `_THRESHOLDS` with a first-run MRV2 triage policy (contract-layer failure = bug; mechanism-layer failure = baseline comparison first, split per runner only for proven-legitimate shifts)
- includes the #44483 partial-wake scheduler regression test: the scheduler must hold requests between `wake_up(["weights"])` and `wake_up(["kv_cache"])` instead of dispatching FlashAttention on the unmapped kv_cache VA

Per-dimension breakdown:

| Dimension | Class | Tests |
|---|---|---|
| state flags + `vllm:engine_sleep_state` metrics | TestSleepWakeFlags | 5 |
| physical GPU bytes freed/re-allocated per level | TestPhysicalMemory | 4 |
| scheduler gate during partial wake | TestSchedulerGate | 3 |
| golden output after full/staged wake + cycles | TestOutputCorrectness | 4 |
| protocol misuse tolerance | TestErrorPaths | 3 |
| concurrent generate vs sleep/wake liveness | TestConcurrentRace | 1 |
| GPU memory stability across 10 cycles | TestMemoryLeakCycle | 1 |
| n>1 in-flight abort drains cleanly | TestAbortDuringParallelSampling | 1 |
| logprobs drift < 1e-2 | TestLogprobsPrecision | 1 |
| latency bounds (full/staged/cycles) | TestSleepWakeLatency | 3 |
| 5 staged cycles output stability | TestStagedWakeCycles | 1 |

Resolves (test coverage for) the regression introduced by #44483. RFC: #45585.

## Test Plan

```bash
# Requires a GPU; default model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B (override via VLLM_TEST_MODEL)
pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/test_sleep_wake.py -v

# Single runner round
pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/test_sleep_wake.py -v -k MRV1
pytest tests/entrypoints/serve/dev/rlhf/test_sleep_wake.py -v -k MRV2
```

## Test Result

- [ ] The test plan, such as providing test command.

items.title: [RFC]: Truncate mode for `thinking_token_budget`
items.body:
### Motivation.

`thinking_token_budget` currently enforces the budget by forcing the logits of
`reasoning_end_str` (e.g. `</think>`) once the reasoning block reaches the budget, then
letting the model continue with the answer. That make sense for general serving but is not ideal for RL
rollouts:

- The forced tokens are not sampled from the policy, so they are off-policy tokens in the
  trajectory and their logprobs are polluted by the 1e9 logit override.
- There is no signal that the budget was hit; the response finishes with the usual
  `finish_reason="stop"`.
- RL trainers typically want an over-budget sample to end right there, be marked as
  truncated (`finish_reason="length"`), and free its KV cache instead of generating an answer

### Proposed Change.

Add an engine-wide flag to `ReasoningConfig`:

```python
thinking_budget_action: Literal["force_end", "truncate"] = "force_end" # keeps current behavior as default
```

```bash
vllm serve ... --reasoning-config '{ ... "thinking_budget_action": "truncate"}'
```

With `thinking_budget_action=truncate`:

- The budget is enforced in the scheduler, not the sampler. A small tracker on
  `Request` (reasoning start position, reasoning token count) is updated per output token
  in `_update_request_with_output`, using the start and natural-end token ids already
  derived by `ReasoningConfig.initialize_token_ids`. Prompt-resident reasoning tokens
  are counted at request creation, as the current implementation does.
- `check_stop` add one conditional branch next to the `max_tokens` check: when the count reaches
  the budget the request is finished with a new `RequestStatus.FINISHED_THINKING_BUDGET`,
  mapped to `FinishReason.LENGTH`, with `stop_reason="thinking_token_budget"`. No new
  `FinishReason` value, so API and Rust DTOs are unchanged.
- The sampler-side engines are disabled at construction in this mode
  (`maybe_create_thinking_budget_state_holder` returns `None`; V2 `ThinkingBudgetState`
  is constructed disabled). No token is ever forced.
- Speculative decoding and async scheduling need no special handling: the existing
  per-token stop loop already trims tokens after a stop, and the one-step lag is the same as
  for `max_tokens`.

List of affected files (probably): `vllm/config/reasoning.py`, `vllm/v1/request.py`,
`vllm/v1/core/sched/utils.py`, one condition each in `gpu_input_batch.py` and
`gpu/sample/thinking_budget.py`, docs in `reasoning_outputs.md`, unit tests in
`tests/v1/core` and an e2e case in `test_thinking_token_budget.py`.


### Feedback Period.

_No response_

### CC List.

_No response_

### Any Other Things.

🤚 happy to contribute this feature if accepted! I already have a working implementation 

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Model] Qwen4Exp: fp8_e4m3 and nvfp4 KV cache on the QSA path
items.body:
## Purpose

Let the QSA layers of Qwen4Exp (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) run with `--kv-cache-dtype fp8_e4m3` or `nvfp4`. Today the path hard-refuses anything but bf16 (`Qwen4Exp QSA requires a BF16 main KV cache`), although the write path (`reshape_and_cache_flash`), the KV spec (`kv_quant_mode`) and the per-layer scales are already in place. What was missing is the read side of the sparse paged GQA Triton kernel and a set of guards.

Related: #54426 (RFC with an independent fp8_e4m3 implementation on GB10, corroborated on a second GB10). This PR was developed independently on SM120 and adds nvfp4; the four integration points named there match what we hit (uint8 storage, inherited `FlashAttentionImpl` guard, shared-memory limit, indexer cache). One difference: here the indexer caches stay bf16 by construction and the selector path is not touched.

**What the change does**

- `ops/qsa.py`: two compile-time branches in `_qsa_sparse_paged_gqa_splitk_kernel` (`KV_QUANT_FP8`, `KV_QUANT_NVFP4`), compiled out for bf16.
  - fp8_e4m3: upcast the tile to the query dtype, apply the per-layer scale, cast back before `tl.dot` (Triton cannot multiply fp8e4nv on SM12x).
  - nvfp4: K and V in separate head slots of `head_size // 2 + head_size // 16` bytes (E2M1 data plus E4M3 block scales, one per 16 values). E2M1 unpack and block-scale lookup happen in the kernel; block scales are loaded at their natural width `[HEAD_DIM // 16, BLOCK_N]` and broadcast in registers. K block scales are stored linearly, V block scales swizzled, the layout the native writer produces (measured, see tests).
  - Quantized wide (prefill) tiles run with one pipeline stage: on SM120 the fp8 branch at `BLOCK_N=64` with two stages requested 106496 B against a 101376 B limit. The nvfp4 wide tile is 32 (1.7x faster than 64 at one stage on SM120; two stages at 64 were slower, occupancy-bound). The decode profile (`BLOCK_N=16`) is unchanged.
- `nvidia/qsa.py`: accept `fp8`, `fp8_e4m3`, `nvfp4`; `customize_spec` and `get_kv_cache_spec` apply the nvfp4 page geometry (same as `FlashInferBackend.customize_spec`); `get_kv_cache_shape` and an HND stride order for nvfp4 (under NHD the K/V head slots interleave and `nvfp4_split_data_scale` would overlap data and scales); an own `do_kv_cache_update` that cuts the packed cache by head slot; the inherited FlashAttention capability checks are bypassed because QSA never reads its main cache with a FlashAttention kernel. Quantized caches are reinterpreted from `uint8` right before the kernel. The indexer caches stay bf16 (`QSAKeyStateCache` packs int64 mRoPE positions into bf16 cells).
- `platforms/interface.py`: the hybrid page alignment falls back to the nvfp4 geometry when the resolved backend does not customize the spec. Without it the block size is aligned against a page that does not exist. This is the one change outside the model directory; happy to move it if there is a better place.

Not included on purpose: `fp8_e5m2` (smaller mantissa, no benefit for K/V), `nvfp4_4over6` (changes the block-scale search in the writer, not evaluated on this path), calibrated per-layer scales (scale 1.0 measured 0.0000 % saturation and underflow on this checkpoint, quality gates at parity), the AMD QSA mirror (`amd/qsa.py`, same guards, untouched).

## Test Plan

New numerical tests in `tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_kv_quant.py`:

- fp8 and nvfp4 kernel output against a float64 PyTorch reference computed on the *dequantized* cache contents (measures the kernel, not the quantization), plus kernel-vs-kernel across all tile profiles of the wrapper (2 / 5 / 64 / 200 / 300 query rows, i.e. `BLOCK_N=16` two stages and the wide one-stage profiles).
- nvfp4 layout probe: the cache is written with `reshape_and_cache_flash("nvfp4")` and unpacked under all four block-scale hypotheses (K linear/swizzled x V linear/swizzled); the assumed layout must be the one with pure rounding error.
- bf16 path bitwise identical with and without the scale arguments.

```bash
pytest tests/models/qwen4_exp/test_qsa_kv_quant.py -v
```

End-to-end (not part of CI): paired runs on one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120, 96 GB), `RadixArk/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4`, TP1, MTP off, same checkpoint and start line, only `--kv-cache-dtype` varied, bf16 control run on the same day. Done on the `vllm/vllm-openai:qwen38-flash-next` build (`0.1.dev20073+g8e685d198`, module then named `qwen3_8_flash_next`); the QSA files of that build are identical to `main` apart from the module rename, and the cleaned code in this PR was re-run through the numerical tests on that build before submitting.

## Test Result

Numerical tests: `13 passed in 54 s` on SM120 (this PR's code, run on the `qwen38-flash-next` build with the module name mapped back). Values: fp8 kernel error 2.10e-3 relative vs 2.09e-3 for the bf16 kernel against the same reference; nvfp4 2.09e-3 vs 2.08e-3; all tile profiles within 1.3e-4 (fp8) and 4.9e-4 (nvfp4) max abs of the bf16 kernel on dequantized values; layout probe K linear / V swizzled at 0.090 relative error, every wrong hypothesis at 1.32; bf16 bitwise stable.

End-to-end, fp8_e4m3, scales 1.0:

| | bf16 | fp8_e4m3 | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| KiB per token, main KV (engine pool line) | 25.451 | **13.477** | x1.889 |
| KV pool at identical VRAM | 535,178 tokens | **1,010,693** | x1.889 |
| GSM8K, paired, n=100 | 97/100 | 96/100 | McNemar p = 1.0000, one discordant pair |
| Perplexity, three corpora, 1.49 M tokens | | +0.116 / -0.063 / -0.031 % | all CIs include 0; run-to-run self-difference +0.0995 % |
| Needle in a haystack, 65k to 235k | 50/50 | **70/70** | exhaustion 0.0 % |
| Decode, two prompt classes | 86.0 / 83.8 t/s | 85.3 / 82.5 t/s | -0.8 % / -1.6 % |
| Prefill, true cache miss, 12.8k tokens | 10,326 t/s | 9,724 t/s | -5.8 % |

End-to-end, nvfp4, scales 1.0:

| | nvfp4 | vs bf16 | vs fp8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| KiB per token, main KV | **8.320** | x3.059 | x1.62 |
| KV pool at identical VRAM | **1,637,114** tokens | x3.059 | x1.62 |
| GSM8K, paired, n=100 | p = 1.0000 | | zero discordant pairs |
| Needle in a haystack | 70/70 | | |
| Perplexity | **+0.37 to +0.59 % worse**, consistent, all CIs exclude 0 | | 3.4 to 6x above run-to-run noise |
| Prefill | | | 1.75x slower at short context, 2.00x at 1M |
| Decode | flat, under 2 % | | |

nvfp4 is not free on this model: the perplexity penalty is real and does not show on the task axes we ran. Open item: on aggregation tasks near 1M our vLLM nvfp4 path scored 6/12 where SGLang on the same KV precision class scored 8/8 (Fisher exact p = 0.0769). Not resolved; more runs needed.

**Limitations / what reviewers should know**

- One machine, one architecture (SM120). The code has no SM gate (software dequant), but nothing else was measured.
- MTP / speculative decoding and batch scaling were not part of the gate chain.
- Two points where direction from the maintainers would help: (1) whether the platform-level nvfp4 fallback in `interface.py` is the right place, and (2) whether a QSA-local dequant helper (as here) or reuse of `_cast_kv_tile` from `triton_unified_attention.py` (the approach in #54426) is preferred. Either is a small change.

Code and full measurement write-up: https://github.com/andreasgru/vllm-qwen38-flash-next-kv-quant
